posts.title: MSVC Build Tools Version 14.52 Release Candidate Now Available
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
We are pleased to announce the availability of the release candidate for Microsoft C++ (MSVC) Build Tools version 14.52. With this release, C++23 is ready for production use and available through the /std:c++23 compiler option; see below for details. This is the last MSVC v14.52 preview before it moves to stable status and full support. You can download it from the Visual Studio 2026 Insiders Channel. As this is the release candidate, it is now the default toolset installed with C++ workloads in this channel. To check if it’s installed simply make sure one or both of these components are checked in the installer:
MSVC Build Tools for x64/x86 (Latest)
MSVC Build Tools for ARM64/ARM64EC (Latest)
The version number printed by cl.exe and link.exe will be at least 14.52.37025 / 19.52.37025.
We appreciate any feedback that you may have. Please report any issues on Visual Studio Developer Community so we can address them by the time we move out of preview.
Version 14.52 is expected to go stable in November and will ship with the 18.12 release of Visual Studio (Stable Channel).
This post summarizes the work done by the MSVC team between the 14.51 and 14.52 releases. This encompasses changes across the compiler frontend, backend, linker, standard library, and related tools.
C++ standards conformance
C++23 language mode: Use /std:c++23 to select C++23 language rules. The existing /std:c++23preview spelling still works and is an alias for /std:c++23. The preview form is now deprecated and will be removed in a future update.
Immediate escalation: C++23 immediate escalation (P2564R3) lets eligible constexpr functions and lambdas become immediate when their use requires it. It is enabled in C++23 and later modes; C++20 builds can opt in with /Zc:immediateEscalation.
Unicode identifiers: C++23 and C23 modes recognize the mathematical compatibility identifier ranges from P3658R1.
Constexpr allocation in modules: Module interfaces can represent constexpr functions that contain new T[n] expressions.
Preprocessor behavior: _Pragma works in more macro-expansion cases and is supported under /E.
Constexpr cmath: Support for C++ compile-time cmath functions remains off-by-default under /std:c++23 and may be enabled via the /Zc:cmath switch. Please see https://devblogs.microsoft.com/cppblog/msvc-c23-constexpr-cmath-with-llvm-libc/ for additional details.
C++/CLI, C, and language tooling
/clr is now available in C++23 and later modes.
The opt-in /Zc:functionToObjectPtr switch rejects implicit conversions from function pointers to void*.
The compiler now accepts selected constexpr constructor-template instantiations involving virtual base classes. Constructing those virtual bases during constant evaluation remains unsupported, so this is limited to the declaration checks for a constexpr function.
In C code, C4815 and C4816 now warn when a structure is allocated without storage for its flexible array member or when a structure with a flexible array member is passed by value.
The Linux C++ IntelliSense parser maps C++20 and C++23 standard options to the corresponding language modes.
Argument-dependent lookup now handles more names that are not exported from a module, and nested template and module instantiation is less prone to failure.
Module serialization preserves class data members and template information more consistently. Type merging also works better when several modules share a header unit.
Header units preserve macro whitespace so stringized macros survive a round trip. Module processing also handles types first defined in the global module fragment more reliably.
Math intrinsics and math headers now work more consistently with modules and constant evaluation.
Caret diagnostics use less memory, and several diagnostics reproduce the original source expression more accurately.
Preprocessor diagnostics better identify malformed and nested constant expressions.
The compiler handles invalid type-trait inputs and malformed function-parameter scopes more consistently.
The compiler warns when overriding a deprecated non-pure virtual function.
Code generation and optimization
Inlining:
LTCG now considers which fields of a small return object the caller reads, so inlining can discard work that computes unused fields.
Whole-program optimization can favor an inline when doing so exposes parts of a local object and makes unused stores removable.
A large outlined loop body can now inline through a small wrapper called from a loop.
With PGO, small size-optimized virtual-call targets can be speculatively inlined when the profile, size, and growth limits allow it.
The inliner follows function-pointer values through aggregate assignments, preserving more indirect-call opportunities in template adapters.
Type-based devirtualization now works alongside profile-guided inlining. Hot/cold information also does more to prevent cold code from being pulled into hot callers.
Loop and scalar optimization:
The compiler can move more invariant loads out of loops after proving that each load executes on every iteration and remains safe across aliased pointers.
Equality-tested loops shed more loop-carried work, and strength reduction handles more wrapping integer induction expressions.
When three or more multiplications share a divisor, the optimizer can compute one reciprocal and reuse it instead of restoring repeated divisions.
Copy propagation through aliased fields is on by default and understands known-size memcpy and memset operations.
x64 conditional selection handles more nonzero constants and safe aliased operands.
Unsigned comparisons and induction-variable ranges now establish more nonzero, ordering, and non-overflow facts for later optimization.
Scalar conditional expressions gain more value-equivalence, incoming-value, multiply, and shift simplifications.
Calls use restrict arguments more precisely when determining memory interference, exposing more optimization around those calls.
The x86 optimizer performs more local and cross-block copy propagation.
The compiler recognizes more rotate idioms and dynamic bit-field extraction controls, and removes redundant POPCNT zero extension.
Small-aggregate optimization removes padding-only assignments, decomposes qualifying whole-struct loads, and forwards eligible loads through local memcpy operations.
Constant conversions can fold without /fp:fast when the transformation is otherwise valid.
Earlier loop-invariant motion and broader expression reassociation expose more work to later optimization.
Larger functions reuse more repeated expressions. Min/max expressions, mixed-signedness compare diamonds, and repeated vector-element extraction also simplify in more cases.
More indirect calls to noexcept functions become tail calls. Static constant arrays can also disappear when their storage is unnecessary.
Loop unswitching handles more nested-loop cases before vectorization, while straight-line vectorization handles more merged values.
Jump chains and induction variables simplify in more cases without losing useful predicates or signedness information.
The compiler emits less attribute data, scans exception regions fewer times, bounds pathological dead-use searches, and processes large chained function expressions in linear rather than quadratic time.
Vectorization:
On x64 and ARM64, the compiler vectorizes more code that selects values through branches.
Integer reductions such as sum += a[i] - b[i] can be reassociated into a form the loop vectorizer recognizes.
On x64 and ARM64, vector loads and stores reach copy propagation and scalar replacement earlier. Full-width vectors remain intact when splitting them would discard useful vector operations.
The vectorizer recognizes more adjacent-address patterns and is more willing to pack user-written SIMD values when the result can remain in a vector register.
A parameter-derived pointer advanced by a loop is recognized as non-aliasing a local array in more cases, avoiding an unnecessary runtime overlap check.
The loop vectorizer handles qualifying memory-only swaps and multi-stream copies, including std::swap on arrays of trivial types.
More loop-control expressions shared by a following conditional simplify after the loop.
ARM64
ARM64 now shares address calculations across related loads and stores, including array-of-structures loops based on function parameters. This removes repeated arithmetic and creates more opportunities for paired loads and stores.
Known NEON constants can be built without unnecessary data loads. Scalar loads, broadcasts, and lane inserts also fold into NEON load instructions in more cases.
The compiler combines more NEON construction and lane operations, removes unused lane inserts, and eliminates redundant mask comparisons.
The loop vectorizer now handles additional floor, ceil, trunc, and round operations.
Tail-call decisions are now made per call, so one ineligible call no longer blocks another eligible call in the same function.
ARM64 and ARM64EC inlining accounts for floating-point and vector register pressure. This preserves profitable native ARM64 inlines while avoiding excessive spills on restricted ARM64EC targets.
Native ARM64 SVE2 supports code generation and disassembly for lane-indexed svmullb and svmullt intrinsics. Execution requires SVE2-capable hardware.
LUTI2 and LUTI4 lookup-table support includes BF16 forms. Floating-point absolute minimum/maximum instructions and Common Short Sequence Compression operations are also supported. Each family requires the corresponding processor feature.
ARM64_FPMR names the FPMR register for _ReadStatusReg and _WriteStatusReg; armasm64 and the disassembler recognize the same name. Execution requires FEAT_FPMR hardware and OS permission.
Native ARM64 supports __preserve_none and [[msvc::musttail]], including specialized interpreter dispatch. The __preserve_none calling convention is C-only and is not supported on ARM64EC.
With /feature:sme, the compiler accepts SME attributes and ZA-state types on supported external declarations. Eligible scalar noexcept calls can perform the required streaming-mode transitions, including selected function-pointer, reference, whole-program, and Control Flow Guard cases. Streaming function definitions, ZA-bearing calls, unsupported pointer forms, and vector or aggregate arguments remain unsupported. ARM64EC is excluded.
The native ARM64 CRT supplies the AAPCS64 SME state-management routines for TPIDR2, ZA, and ZT0. Availability depends on processor and operating-system state support; ARM64EC is excluded.
On ARM64, the /Zc:cmath math runtime now supports the floating-point environment. This initial implementation reports math errors through floating-point exceptions rather than errno.
ARM64 stack layout can reuse slots for locals in mutually exclusive switch cases, greatly reducing the frame size of large switches.
Stateless SVE all-true predicates can move out of loops when the usual safety and profitability checks allow it.
Proven-dead switch edges are removed before switch expansion, exposing more control-flow and value optimizations.
Bitfield operations use narrower immediate forms where possible.
Register assignment preserves more adjacent load pairs and makes better spill/rematerialization choices for frequently used values.
Used-lane tracking now crosses more scalar floating-point operations, exposing dead vector work.
The compiler recognizes more vector permutations, per-lane rotations, and vector bit-clear immediate forms.
SVE comparisons and the MATCH/NMATCH/WHILE families reuse condition flags more effectively. NEON-to-SVE bridge moves, upper-lane float extraction, and by-element multiply addressing also produce shorter sequences.
x64 and x86
Speed-optimized x64 builds have more strategies for fixed-length memcmp. Eligible copies larger than 256 bytes use the runtime copy path instead of a large inline sequence.
x64 removes more redundant zero extensions before jump-table address calculations and lowers unsigned division by a constant power of two to a shift.
Constant f64x2 assignments can combine so a later vector operation folds to one 128-bit constant move.
32-bit x86 builds can inline fmin, fmax, and copysign; ARM64 can inline copysign.
AVX2 and AVX-512 targets can build wider vectors from smaller register values without a memory round trip.
AVX-512 code generation uses suitable VEX moves for intrinsic operands and folds eligible single-use masked arithmetic followed by a blend into one merge-masked operation.
Builds using /feature:APX gain more arithmetic and conditional-selection forms, fewer redundant moves and comparisons, and APX-aware unrolling and strength-reduction decisions for scalar integer loops.
APX support now spans the ABI, assembler, disassembler, and debugging tools. R30 and R31 are nonvolatile, register assignment treats them as killed across setjmp, MASM and the disassembler handle eligible extended-register encodings, and DIA reads APX register context.
APX-enabled x64 code generation can fold eligible operands and makes better spill, recomputation, and fold choices.
Unwind V3 support now spans code generation, linking, ML64, DIA, and binary instrumentation. It covers chained runtime-function records, large prologs and epilogs, .PUSHFRAME/.POPFRAME, and stack walking. ML64 requires /unwindv3; compiler emission is on by default only for APX functions, and stack walking requires a V3-aware operating system and debugger.
x64 recognizes more condition-code-safe INC/DEC forms, including eligible atomic fetch-add sequences.
AVX2 intrinsic lowering removes unnecessary scalar-to-vector moves in qualifying _mm_set_sd and _mm256_set1_pd paths.
APX code generation includes more new-destination and memory-operand forms, shorter LEA replacements for eligible INC/DEC and SUB sequences, and broader shift, compare, conditional-compare, conditional-move, and constant-propagation support.
All-bits-set vector constants and functions containing paired register operations receive better code generation.
Shift-range analysis models the hardware shift-count mask, and adjacent two-element double stores combine more effectively.
Under /O1 and /Os, additional pre-allocation optimizations and size-aware instruction costs reduce code size.
RDPRU uses its required fixed-register constraints.
Standard Library
See the STL Changelog – MSVC Build Tools 14.52 for a complete list of all of the changes in this release, grouped by features, LWG issue resolutions, bug fixes, performance improvements, etc. Some highlights:
The STL is C++23 feature complete now that P0533R9 “constexpr For <cmath> And <cstdlib>” has been implemented.

This is initially supported for MSVC only, under /std:c++23 /Zc:cmath. We expect to make /std:c++23 imply /Zc:cmath in a future release, but it is currently opt-in. Clang and EDG support will be enabled when the necessary compiler machinery becomes available.
For more info, read MSVC C++23: constexpr cmath with LLVM Libc by Cody Miller (MSVC compiler front-end dev) and Bringing Correctly Rounded Math to Production with LLVM-libc by Michael Jones and Tue Ly (LLVM-libc maintainers at Google).
And under /std:c++latest /Zc:cmath, we’ve mostly implemented C++26 P1383R2 ‘s constexpr additions for <cmath>. (No <complex> changes yet.) A few functions are not yet implemented by LLVM-libc (see LLVM libc math status ) and accordingly are not yet constexpr. For double, the functions acosh, asinh, atanh, cosh, sinh, tanh, and erf are missing. For float and double, the functions erfc, lgamma, and tgamma are missing. (MSVC uses 64-bit long double, so we don’t need a third implementation of each function.) As soon as they become available, we’ll activate them as constexpr in future releases.
19 LWG issue resolutions, which are bugfixes in the Standard.

We track every LWG issue that’s resolved in the Standard in our STL LWG Issues project .
Improved <regex> performance in several scenarios.

Special thanks to Julian Müller (@muellerj2 on GitHub) for this ongoing correctness and performance overhaul of <regex>.
Added ARM64 SVE vectorized implementations of several STL algorithms.

Also fixed regressions and improved performance in some of the ARM64/ARM64EC Neon vectorized implementations that were previously added.
Special thanks to Hari Limaye at Arm (@hazzlim on GitHub) for this ongoing vectorization work.
AddressSanitizer
Improved runtime performance by removing duplicated quarantine work
Use MSDIS (MSVC disassembler) as a fallback instruction-length decoder for interception, reducing “unrecognized instruction” failures. This is on by default and can be disabled via ASAN_OPTIONS=windows_use_msdis_decoder=false . To trace what instructions were intercepted by MSDIS instead of the manual instruction decoder, set verbosity=3 and search for logs prefixed with “MSDIS instruction decoder:”.
Runtime performance improvements including heap address caching, more efficient memory-mapped heap checks, and faster allocator flag assignments, resulting in significant performance gains across multiple runtime scenarios.
Build tools and diagnostics
The C++ frontend accepts more valid designated-initialization forms.
The C++ frontend accepts more deeply nested initializers, and the legacy preprocessor allows larger macro buffers.
Code Analysis SARIF output includes rule names, descriptions, and help links by default, plus tags where available.
LNK2022 and LNK4227 name the relevant metadata item. LNK4323 explains a missing ARM64EC/native object pair.
Incremental linking trims excess growth space from program-database files.
The disassembly library recognizes MIPS32 and MIPS64 Release 6 instructions and ARM64 matrix-state start/stop instructions.
/analyze:log:format:sarifandxml writes both Code Analysis log formats.
LNK4321 identifies duplicate C++ module exports while generating an import library.
C5089 identifies the experimental combination of /fsanitize=address with /clr, including /clr:netcore.
In C++, two new level-4 warnings diagnose implicit and explicit conversions between HRESULT/SCODE and bool-like types. They are off by default and do not apply to C.
The opt-in /PDB4GBSTREAMS option raises the size limit for the PDB global/public symbol-record stream to roughly 4 GiB. Other PDB streams retain their existing limits.
MASM and the disassembly library recognize the x86 int1/ICEBP instruction (0xF1).
LTCG emits C4744 when extern declarations disagree on type.
PE reproducibility improves because the image hash no longer includes the PDB age.
Tag-based Code Analysis warning groups simplify ruleset authoring.
Debugger clients can release a program-database file handle without discarding loaded data, allowing the file to be rebuilt sooner. Debug information also merges module and header-unit types more reliably.
Debug records can identify alternate object names, and type-record processing performs fewer allocations and improves throughput on large programs.
Linker and assembler diagnostics are clearer, and malformed object files, libraries, and module metadata are handled more defensively.

posts.title: How Meta Built Forum With AI-Native Engineering
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
Meta’s newest app, Forum, is for anyone who wants to go deeper into the conversations in their Facebook groups.
To build Forum, Meta engineers adopted a whole new way of working by bringing an AI agent into the development cycle.
We’re sharing insights into what it took to build Forum with agentic AI: how we adapted the codebase, tested frameworks and internal tooling for agentic execution, what worked, and what didn’t.
Forum is a standalone Groups app that a small team built from scratch. It’s also where we tested a different way of working: treating an AI agent as a participant in the engineering process rather than a faster way to type.
That experiment needed a definition of success, and ours wasn’t code volume. We measured verified, production-ready outcomes — changes that build, pass tests, and survive review. 
From Human-In-The-Loop to Human-On-The-Loop
Pointing AI at the coding step alone doesn’t change much. Our results compounded as we extended the approach to the stages around implementation — planning, building, testing, and verification. The clearest way to see the shift is in who owns each step.
With human-in-the-loop, the engineer drives every step and the AI assists inside it by autocompleting a function, suggesting a fix, or answering a question. Each iteration advances at the pace of the person driving it.
With human-on-the-loop, the agent runs the iteration itself — plan, implement, build, test, correct, repeat — while the engineer sets the goal, watches the run, steps in when it drifts, and approves the result. The person’s job moves from executing the steps to owning the outcome and holding the quality bar. This is the target we are driving toward, not a finished state: some stages run autonomously today, while others still keep an engineer in each iteration.
When the engineer supervises, work stops being strictly sequential. Cycles that used to run one at a time can overlap, and an engineer’s time goes to direction and judgment rather than to sitting through the loop. But that only holds if what comes back can be trusted. Without verification, AI-generated code creates a familiar problem — plausible output that no one has confirmed actually works, which an engineer then has to read, debug, and often discard. Weak signals don’t remove the constraint; they move it from writing code to reviewing code that looks finished and isn’t.
So we set the bar at verification rather than compilation. Compiling isn’t the finish line — a task is complete only once automated tests and visual checks have passed. Agents check their own work before an engineer sees it, which means what reaches review is a smaller set of higher-confidence results rather than a pile of output to sift through. Less gets generated, and less gets discarded. Every shipped outcome still carries an engineer’s sign-off; our effort went into making that sign-off fast and well-evidenced, with build results, test outcomes, and recorded verification sessions attached to the change.
With the engineer outside of every cycle, the loop has to run safely on its own. Four capabilities make that possible:

Planning as technical specification: Agentic execution requires extreme precision. Ambiguity that an engineer might resolve through intuition results in agent failure. We invested in rigorous upstream decomposition and machine-readable context, which tightened the engineering loop for engineers and agents alike.
Automated verification inside the loop is the force multiplier: We integrated automated pass/fail signals — build status, unit tests, and UI spec matching — directly into the agent loop. This enabled asynchronous development producing ready-to-review pull requests with pre-populated test plans and recorded verification sessions. Verification is the hard part to get right, and how much we can safely hand to the loop is gated by how much we can trust the verifiers.
Simulated user testing with agents: We deployed navigation agents that interact with the live app exactly like a person would. These agents perform actions, read the screen, and report regressions. Navigation agents are able to run the same verification paths continuously. 
Agentic production operations: After launch, agents help automate root-cause analysis. When someone using Forum submits feedback, the agents use that feedback to investigate possible regressions. The agents then forward the analysis to engineers who decide the next course of action.  
The Operating Model
That ownership model needs machinery with five key components:
Rules are permanent project instructions. When the agent repeats a mistake more than twice, we encode the correction once, for everyone.
Skills turn team conventions into loadable steps the agent can invoke.
Agents automate checks that previously required a manual pass. 
Commands chain skills and agents into workflows. They assess complexity, reproduce a bug, plan and implement a fix, create the pull request, and run a multi-stage review.
Hooks are automated triggers, such as running a linter after every agent turn, checking simulator connectivity before install, and validating tests before a pull request is created.
Adapting the Environment to the Models
The biggest gains came from changing our code and tooling, not our prompts. 
Architectural legibility over inherited complexity: We worked to keep Forum’s codebase as straightforward as possible and chose to modularize key pieces of the architecture in order to get the benefits of battle-tested infrastructure while also letting the agents plug and play easily. Where we couldn’t easily do so, we rebuilt from scratch, trading reuse for agentic throughput, and it proved rewarding in development speed. Agents learn patterns from the code they read. Fix a weak pattern once and every future agent session inherits the improvement; leave it and the same shortcut shows up in everything the agent writes next. 
Give agents tools, not descriptions: Our main failure mode was the agent losing track of where it was in the app — editing the home feed when asked to change the group home screen, or guessing at screen coordinates. So instead of describing the app to the agent, we gave it tools to check: read the live view hierarchy from the simulator, list the elements actually on screen, and look up the path to a target view — all before it acts. Misdirected edits dropped sharply. We applied the same approach wherever agents touched our systems: give the agent a way to check state directly rather than a description to reason from.
Build-level isolation for safe AI prototyping: As Forum matured toward production, we wanted early-stage prototypes and agent-generated experiments to have room to run while keeping the production app strictly limited to finished, reviewed work. We wanted a stronger guarantee than feature gating alone, where prototype code still exists inside the production build. Our solution was a separate build flavor, a sandbox app that shares the exact same codebase, frameworks, and design system as production, but compiles prototype code out of the production build entirely via a plugin/socket architecture. 
This gave us three things at once: 
Designers and cross-functional partners could prototype freely using AI tools without needing an engineer in the loop for each change. 
Anything built in the sandbox could be ported directly to production with no rebuild. 
No prototype code could crash the production app because it physically didn’t exist in that build. 
The pattern let us keep fast AI iteration after we had real people using the app to protect.
Finding Real Bugs With AI Stress Testing
Adapting the environment did more than make the agent faster to build with — it made the agent a tester. We didn’t point it at one specific defect. Instead, we set up repeatable stress scenarios that mimic real user behavior (aggressive scrolling, random group browsing, rapid navigation, repeated media loading) and ran them routinely across builds. Because these runs produce consistent signals (crashes, memory growth, page faults, UI regressions), the agent can triage anomalies, narrow to the triggering sequence, and then investigate the root cause.
One such run surfaced a memory issue. The agent isolated a repro, proposed a fix, and verified it — all during development, before the app reached users. The fix materially reduced on-device memory growth and page faults across repeated stress sessions.
While engineers made the architectural decisions, the detection and regression monitoring were automated and repeatable; once an anomaly was detected, the agent could reproduce → isolate → propose a fix → verify with the same harness.
Applying the Same Discipline to Forum’s Feed
We applied the human-on-the-loop approach in two places:
Building the stack: Agents mapped the architectural options and trade-offs; engineers then evaluated and chose. What we deliberately kept human was the target — deciding what a good outcome looks like is a product judgment, not something the system should define for itself.
Operating the stack: Questions that used to require whichever engineer knew the relevant code path now go to an investigation agent that gathers what it needs and posts a write-up with suggested fixes. After hand-scoring a batch of real investigations we arrived at a workflow where the agent compresses the mechanical work and delivers a structured write-up to an engineer, who then validates whether a finding is a real bug or an intentional trade-off. 
What improved quality wasn’t better prompting. It was context. One recurring category of investigation came back weak until we gave the agent the same pointers to the relevant code, example queries, and design docs that we’d give any new engineer on day one. The quality of that category jumped. The difference from human onboarding is that you train once, and every future session starts from it.

Did It Work?
Beyond shipping faster, we shipped cleaner. Continuous verification surfaced systemic issues — like the memory bottleneck above — during development rather than after launch. The results show up in the performance profile:


Quality, found early: The autonomous stress-testing loop caught and fixed the aforementioned memory issue during development rather than post-launch, roughly halving memory use and page faults.
Velocity: Forum reached core feature parity with Facebook Groups in eight weeks, with AI handling much of the routine implementation so engineers could focus on architecture, product decisions, and quality.
Leverage that lasted: After launch, agent-driven investigation helped engineers triage and root-cause user feedback. 
The AI did more than generate code. It tightened our quality loop, helping a small team deliver a high-quality app with less ongoing rework.
What Worked, and What Did Not
 
Acknowledgements 
We thank Neeharika Sinha, Jane Kou, Gang Yang, Guohao Zhang, Zeya Zhang, Kinnary Jangla, andYonghui Lu for their valuable contributions.

posts.title: 2026 World Cup: Breaking Records, Spiky Charts and Reliability at Scale
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
Every four years, the World Cup becomes the largest planned stress test of our infrastructure. This year it also set an all-time record!
There are a few moments throughout the year, like New Years Eve, that really let us see the collective impact of everything we’ve built — but none are bigger than the quadrennial World Cup tournament. The 2026 World Cup broke records across messaging, video, recommendations, and networking at the same time. 
Some highlights:
WhatsApp: More than 30 million messages per second during the July 19 final (Argentina vs. Spain), 1.23x the peak of New Year’s Eve 2026 and an all-time platform record. The previous record had already fallen 12 days earlier, during the Round of 16 match between Argentina and Egypt, at 29 million messages per second.
Messenger, Threads, and Instagram Direct: 49 million messages per minute at peak.
Instagram: Recommendation system traffic up to 80% higher week-over-week. Final-squad players collectively added +213.6 million activated followers — a 6.6% increase — with combined followings surging from 3.26 billion to 3.47 billion. 
Live video: Watch time spiked +90% on Instagram and +242% on Facebook, versus the July baseline.
Threads: 1.5 billion impressions on tournament-tagged posts, reaching about 15 million people daily and peaking at 25 million on July 6.
Facebook: 80 million posts mentioning the World Cup.
Traffic Followed the Breaks, Not the Ball 
Every World Cup match caused surges in traffic. During the final, for example, traffic surged +46% in about four minutes at the end of regular time, and +57% in about 15 minutes at the final whistle. 
But by lining game events up against global egress traffic we discovered a striking pattern – surges in sharing were primarily happening during breaks (hydration breaks, halftime, extra time, the final whistle, the awards ceremony). The end-of-regulation whistle produced the single biggest peak of the tournament.

It wasn’t the gameplay that moved our charts. It was the conversations after it. The world came to Meta to watch the game and to share what it made them feel. 
Every capacity decision below follows from that one pattern.
Layered Systems, No Manual Intervention
Those spikes were absorbed by systems built for exactly this. Taiji balanced load across datacenters, Katran and Proxygen handled L4/L7 traffic distribution, our global load balancing system routed users to the best-positioned edge, and AutoScaling provisioned capacity on demand.
Region-Specific Capacity
Months before kickoff, Meta’s edge teams analyzed network capacity and worked closely with ISP partners so that upgrades landed where they would most improve quality of experience for end users. That targeted pre-build is now permanent capacity that will keep serving demand long after the tournament.
Instagram: Preparing for 39 Consecutive Days of Surges
For Instagram, the tournament meant 39 straight days of traffic spikes as billions of fans checked scores, posted Stories, and flooded Feed during breaks. Machine learning inference, Feed serving, Stories, Explore, and data infrastructure all had to absorb it without degrading the experience.
During the final, halftime Instagram Feed traffic rose 76% above the previous day in the minute the match ended, and stayed about 21% above for the following two hours.

Our approach rested on four things, deployed incrementally as the tournament moved from group stage to final.
 Capacity buffers: Our products went into the tournament with sufficient capacity, which meant real buffers were available to allocate. We pre-provisioned significant additional capacity across all serving tiers so that spikes never had to wait on autoscaling to catch up. These dedicated buffers were our single most effective lever of the tournament.
 Country-level graceful degradation: For high-risk matches, we shed non-critical background load in the top-traffic nations (Brazil, Argentina, India, Indonesia, Spain) to protect core functionality.
 Cascade prevention: So spikes at the serving layer couldn’t propagate into downstream data systems.
 Early warning signals These alerted us before we approached capacity thresholds, rather than after.
All of this, including the phased deployment timeline and the degradation activation criteria, is now a reusable runbook for future large-scale events like the 2028 Olympics.
WhatsApp: 8.4 Billion Messages in Five Minutes
Goals and the final whistle drove WhatsApp spikes lasting four to five minutes at a time. In its single highest-traffic five-minute window, WhatsApp delivered nearly 8.4 billion messages without interruption.
That came from months of preparation. More than 100 internal services were load-tested and resized ahead of the tournament, then retested, revalidated, and resized as the bracket narrowed and demand climbed.
Two things we’d normally do, we didn’t.
We didn’t shift load between regions. For past high-traffic events, our default has been to spread demand across multiple regions, letting capacity in quieter parts of the world absorb the spike. That works when peaks land hours apart — a global New Year’s Eve, for example. This event was different. Every region peaked in the same instant, so there was no idle capacity to borrow. Instead of deriving regional demand from a global multiplier, we forecast each region’s peak on its own terms.
We didn’t freeze. The other standard playbook move for a major event is to pause continuous deployment and hold off on riskier operations like disaster recovery exercises. This time we skipped the freeze entirely, on the strength of years of reliability enhancement. Teams shipped on their normal cadence throughout the entire event window, including during the peak moment itself. 
We Stay Ready Year-Round
Enabling connection in moments like this doesn’t just happen. Powering every message sent, every follower, and every Reel shared in real time across 48 teams and 104 matches is a story of infrastructure and product working as one.
Capacity planning, load testing, traffic management, and rapid incident response come together across these teams so that billions of people can connect in the moments that matter most — like an entire continent celebrating a last-minute goal at the same second.

posts.title: Sapienz Receives ISSTA 2026 Impact Paper Award
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
Ke Mao, Mark Harman, and Yue Jia have been recognized with the ACM SIGSOFT International Symposium on Software Testing and Analysis (ISSTA) 2026 Most Influential Paper Award for their 2016 research, “Sapienz: multi-objective automated testing for Android applications.” The recognition celebrates a decade of impact from work that began at University College London and went on to become testing infrastructure at Meta.
Sapienz automatically tests apps to find crashes and helps engineers reproduce them in fewer steps, making failures easier to investigate. The original research combined three goals: exploring more of an app, finding more crashes, and reducing the number of steps needed to trigger them. In its evaluation on 1,000 popular Google Play apps, Sapienz found 558 previously unknown crashes.
Within 17 months of publication, Sapienz was deployed at scale at Meta. Today, it runs millions of tests daily across Meta’s platforms, surfaces thousands of unique crashes each week, and helps safeguard hundreds of app releases each month, supporting product reliability and quality.
Sapienz’s applications quickly expanded beyond crash detection. By using test accounts with synthetic conversations, it became the app-exploration engine for dynamic taint analysis at WhatsApp. 
We shared Sapienz’s journey in October in our ISSTA 2026 keynote delivered by Ke Mao, “Finding the Bugs Users Would Find: From Sapienz to Autonomous Agents.” Beyond detecting crashes, large language model (LLM) agents can now explore apps and reason about whether their behavior matches what users should expect, extending automated testing from reliability to functional correctness and, increasingly, automated repair. Sapienz’s core ideas of multi-objective exploration and actionable fault revelation carry over directly. A decade on, those founding principles still hold true.
As part of Meta’s overall privacy and risk management program, this work reflects our ongoing efforts to ensure privacy considerations are at the heart of our product development process, helping teams identify risks earlier in the development lifecycle, apply safeguards more consistently, and build privacy protections into each new innovation from the start.

posts.title: Meta’s Generative Ads Model (GEM): Scaling the Central Model and Compute Engine for Frontier Ads AI
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
Last year, we introduced GEM, the industry’s largest recommendation system (RecSys) foundation model. GEM established Meta’s first LLM-inspired paradigm for ads recommendation, driving major performance gains. Building on this foundation, our next goal is to further scale both compute and intelligence transfer with next-generation hardware, and expand this capability across Meta’s entire ads ecosystem. This spans dozens of surfaces and objectives, delivering seamless full-funnel optimization across awareness, consideration, and conversions. 
The 2026 generation of GEM shifts from isolated per-domain optimizations — such as Facebook, Instagram, Reels — to a single central foundation model. It learns from data and signals across all of Meta’s ads platforms, bends the scaling curve at LLM-scale computation, and delivers strong advertiser outcomes through post-training techniques that provide a larger latency budget without requiring real-time evaluation of all ad candidates — all on a substantially more efficient training stack. The result is simultaneous ad performance gains across every surface and funnel stage, and deeper understanding that better matches ads to what people are looking for.
GEM has delivered 18.9% conversion improvement and 12% ad click-through rate (CTR) improvement across Meta’s ad surfaces and objectives, and additionally contributed 5.8%, 4.1%, and 1.6% conversion uplift on Facebook, Instagram, and off-site conversion for targeted users over the past year. These gains span both upper-funnel surfaces and deep-funnel optimization goals, driving stronger returns for advertisers.

GEM advances the frontier of recommender systems in the following four areas:
1. Bending the Scaling Curve, Enabling 2.5x Model Complexity 
Challenge: Empirical scaling laws demonstrate that model performance predictably improves with compute, parameter, and data size using transformer model architecture. However, recommender system models do not exhibit similar scaling properties with transformer due to massive heterogeneous features and shifting distributions. 
Solution: We built an LLM-style architecture — Kunlun, co-designed with the latest GPU hardware, to make larger, deeper models substantially more cost-efficient and to enable long-context learning over user engagement history. We observed an LLM-like scaling law at our largest pre-training scale with 2.5x model complexity growth from earlier versions of GEM. The pattern mirrors frontier LLMs: more capacity and longer context produce emergent gains in ranking quality that translate directly into business results.
2. Efficient Intelligence Transfer From GEM to User-Facing Models
Challenge: Serving a model at this scale in real time is prohibitively expensive and drives up latency, compromising both user experience and advertiser ROI. 
Solution: The structured representation, LoopFM, a state-of-the-art post-training technique, transfers GEM’s internal representations and sequential historical memory to downstream models. Through computation sharing, it doubles the intelligence transfer together with the knowledge distillation deployed in the previous version, at no additional compute cost or latency. We also introduced elastic pre-computation (Solaris) to harvest the gains from the upstream model.
3. Accelerating the Central Compute Engine With Large-Scale Cross-Surface, Cross-Domain Learning at Meta Ads Scale
Challenge: Meta’s apps span dozens of surfaces — Facebook, Instagram, Reels, Stories, and more — with 3.6 billion people using at least one of our apps each day. Each surface and optimization objective previously had its own independent prediction system. As the platform grows in surfaces and objectives, so does the challenge of improving ad performance simultaneously.
Solution: GEM accelerates one single, unified compute engine through the central foundation model that jointly predicts clicks and conversions across all surfaces, including Facebook and Instagram, and across every key advertiser objective from off-site conversions to mobile app installs. The generalizable representations learned on data-rich click tasks transfer into data-sparse conversion tasks. A new training recipe with cost-free data mixing and the domain expert framework makes this heterogeneous, large-scale learning tractable, with predictable scale and enhanced reliability.
4. Scaling Total Training FLOPs by 4x While Doubling E2E Training Efficiency Across Thousands of GPUs
Challenge: Training a RecSys foundation model across thousands of GPUs at this scale requires careful orchestration of compute, parallelism, communication, and memory. Today’s data center GPUs and their software stacks are mostly optimized for LLM workloads, whereas recommendation workloads have a fundamentally different profile due to unique data characteristics that make it extremely difficult to achieve high GPU compute utilization while scale. 
Solution: We developed custom kernels with low precision and new 5D parallelism strategies co-designed with the latest GPU hardware and Meta’s training cluster, and optimized model architecture with infrastructure together to scale efficiently across thousands of GPUs. End-to-end training efficiency is doubled to 20-25% model FLOPS utilization (MFU) with 4x total training FLOPs, enabling GEM to train at LLM-scale at Meta (see full technical story in our companion blog on Training GEM at LLM Scale).
Scaling Law: Bend Scaling Curve at Frontier Scale with Kunlun
GEM introduces a new LLM-style model architecture — Kunlun. Compared to the previous version (Interformer), Kunlun delivers 2x performance gains with the same computation scaling. Kunlun is designed around the following innovations:
Standardize and unify architecture framework by seamlessly interleaving lifelong sequence modeling with scalable recommendation-specific cross-interaction. 
Introduce scalable architecture through deep co-design with the latest generation of hardware, and computation reduction with almost no model quality regression.
Innovate efficient sequence scaling to process longer user engagement contexts with offline sequence infrastructure.
The scaling law pattern on the light-weight model of GEM with small parameter size.
Efficient Architecture for Scaling Recommendations 
GEM’s Kunlun architecture effectively bends the recommender system scaling curve at frontier training scales by empowering ultra-long user sequences and massive user-item interaction features. For the following technical discussion, we define two types of features: non-sequence features (such as user demographics, ad content representations), and sequence features with a sequence of events, each composed of a set of features. 
This architecture introduces three fundamental advancements:
1. A Standardized and Unified Architecture Framework
We advanced the LLM-style architecture to better capture the unique characteristics of recommender system models — specifically, heterogeneous features and data dynamics. 
Each layer consists of:
Attention: customize the attention and feed-forward networks to capture the long dependency pattern in user behavior by adapting to data dynamics. 
Summarization Component: simplify and enhance the summarization architecture to extract critical user insights from sequences, effectively bridging sequence and non-sequence structure. 
Cross Interaction: expand to the mixture-of-experts (MoE) style design, enabling large-scale modeling of complex interactions between sequence and non-sequence features.


2. Introducing Scalable Architecture Through Deep Co-design
We co-designed the architecture with the latest generation of hardware to allow it to grow deeper and wider efficiently:
Computation Complexity Reduction via Block Attention: Replacing full self-attention with block-aligned sparse attention reduces the complexity associated with sequence length from quadratic to linear relative to window size, and uses only the window size that is a multiple of block size, friendly for the kernel without partial block size.
Component Unification via Architecture Reformulation: Per-Example Feed-Forward Networks (pFFN) was introduced to adapt the traditional FFN to per-example distribution. We reformulated the pFFN component into attention operations through Generalized Dot-Product Attention (GDPA), speeding up training by targeting at unifying the model’s many attention-like operations into a single GPU kernel, delivering up to 2x forward speedup.
Scalable Cross interaction through Expert Parallelism: Our cross-interaction component utilizes a scalable, MoE-like framework that employs model-expert parallelism, allowing each GPU to process a subset of expert sub-networks in parallel.
3. Innovating Efficient Sequence Scaling
We introduced specialized component designs to make ultra-long sequences computationally tractable:
Component Skip Connection (CompSkip): The computational skip mechanism selectively activates sequence modules in each layer, and only routes outputs through residual connections. By selectively deactivating the specific components, which is based on the assumption that the network can recover quickly after re-activating, we reduce FLOPS by 43% with negligible quality loss.
Sequence Unification (OneSeq): We selectively unify user sequences chronologically after the event feature aggregation. This allows a single, unified sequence layer to process long sequences, even when individual events possess heterogeneous structures and features. In the system, we have different user sequence sources, some of which have different events features. For example, an event in a purchase sequence can be described by ad ID and account ID, while the event in a post sequence is described by actors and object ID. They cannot simply be unified from the data source level due to the different set of event features. It requires the flexible sequence unification approach to maximize GPU efficiency because of large-size tensor operations and minimizing operator fragmentation.
The GEM Architecture. On the left is the building block, and right is an illustration of the computation skip mechanism.







How Ultra-Long Sequences Matter
The new architecture makes ultra-long sequences feasible. GEM scaled the long engagement context length by 2x in production, and further enabled the capability of scaling long context to 25x, demonstrating infrastructure capability at frontier scale. Along the way, we discovered:
Prediction quality follows a power law with sequence length. The relationship is predictable and consistent across sequence lengths.
Larger models benefit disproportionately from longer sequences. This creates a virtuous cycle: scaling compute makes the model bigger, which makes longer sequences more valuable. Scaling sequence length makes the model more accurate, which justifies more compute.
The two scaling laws reinforce each other, offering investment directions to bend the overall scaling law curve beyond simply adding compute.
Post-Training: Knowledge Transfer at Scale
The value of the foundation model depends on how effectively its intelligence transfers to the hundreds of vertical models that serve ads in real time. GEM revolutionizes post training for recommendation systems through the structure representation with the deep historical memory from the central brain, achieving 2x of transfer effectiveness beyond knowledge distillation. Furthermore, async computation is introduced to a few domain-specific foundation models to transfer the knowledge to vertical models.
Structure Representation at Scale
Knowledge distillation is effective but limited in bandwidth: downstream models only receive a compressed view of GEM’s intelligence at each training process. To address the limitation, we introduce the precomputed structure representation, such as LoopFM, to understand and compress the central brain from the foundation model into a compact representation, and then structure it with deep historical memory. It enables the downstream models to learn the long context from our central brain. It consists of the following major components across the system: 
Understand and Compress Intelligence: We compress the intelligence from GEM into the compact representations, which are summarized from the important layers, and used to comprehensively describe the event (or data) that is processed by the foundation model. 
Structure with Deep Historical Memory: We structure its compact representation together with the representations that the foundation model previously generated for the same user into a sequential context window, capturing user intent dynamics across all surfaces and traffic through GEM’s memory.
Learn from Long Context Intelligence: Downstream models will learn the structure representation with long historical context through the specialized architecture during both inference and training time.
The representation generation process is precomputed and shared with the computation to generate soft labels of the foundation model for knowledge distillation without additional foundation model cost.
The structure representation paradigm.
Speculative Precomputation for Fresh Predictions
Solaris keeps knowledge transfer fresher, precomputing the user-ad representation from GEM just before vertical model inference needs it. Evaluating the large-scale model inside a live ad request is not affordable, Solaris moves it in time: It speculatively precomputes foundation model embeddings for the user-ad pairs a future request is likely to need, and delivers them just-in-time on the serving hot path. Downstream models gain access to near-real-time foundation model intelligence without being constrained by the latency. Borrowing the idea of speculative decoding from LLM serving, Solaris works through the following major components across the system:
Deliver Fresh Runtime Knowledge: It generates the user-ad embedding directly, giving vertical models real-time, point-to-point knowledge of how a specific user is likely to act on the exact ad candidate. 
Speculate Ahead of the Request: As multi-stage ranking narrows a live request down to its top ad candidates, Solaris evaluates those user-ad pairs with the foundation model in asynchronous background jobs. The computation carries no latency budget with elastic capacity while it can capture rich knowledge.
Enrich Coverage Hierarchically: When an exact user-ad embedding is unavailable, the system degrades rather than drops. It substitutes an aggregate of the user’s own recent embeddings across the same ad groups, or borrows from behaviorally similar users.
Solaris speculative precomputation.
Large-Scale Cross-Domain Optimization: Optimize Across Surfaces and Funnels
We further trained GEM with the ads data at Meta scale, including all-surface data (e.g., Facebook and Instagram Feed and Reels/video) and deep funnel optimization (e.g., off-site conversion, mobile app install). GEM powers the first optimized model that jointly predicts both CTR  across all the surfaces and conversion rate (CVR) across the major optimization goals. Previously, each surface and each prediction objective had its own system. This means learnings from engagement patterns across platforms can more directly be used to understand its conversion behavior (e.g., purchase) across ad surfaces. This positions GEM as the central model and compute engine for ads recommendation across Meta’s advertising surfaces. 
Unlike LLMs with the static data, RecSys models need to deal with data dynamics and freshness as well as the diverse distribution across surfaces and traffic. To overcome the challenge, GEM built the first training recipe for the large-scale cross-surface, cross-domain unification through:
A Cost-Free Data Mixing Strategy: It introduced virtual data loading from different combinations of data pipelines without physically merging data together and incurring additional storage cost. It can flexibly adapt to the current ads ecosystem where the downstream models still train with the specific surface or traffic data. We also design a data mixture mechanism to control the mixture proportions during offline and online training close to the real datastream order received in real time, mitigating instability for domain switch and overmemorization for the recent domain data.
A Domain Expert Framework: A shared expert learns a unified representation across all domains, while domain-specific experts capture surface-specific patterns. Each domain expert benefits from both: the shared cross-domain knowledge and its own specialized knowledge. Experts are built on top of the Kunlun architecture framework.

Training a RecSys Model at LLM-Scale Efficiently
GEM now trains at LLM scale on several thousand of the latest-generation GPUs. Today’s data center GPUs and their software stacks are mostly optimized for LLM workloads, whereas recommendation workloads have a fundamentally different profile due to unique data characteristics and rich user & ads signal interaction patterns that make it extremely difficult to achieve high GPU compute utilization for training a foundational recommendation model of GEM’s size. 
We measure training efficiency through E2E MFU, which decomposes into two factors: E2E MFU = Local MFU (compute efficiency) × Scaling Ratio (scaling efficiency). Local MFU (compute efficiency) measures how well a single GPU’s compute units are utilized — how close the workload runs to the hardware roofline. Scaling Ratio (scaling efficiency) measures how much single-GPU performance is retained when distributing across thousands of GPUs. This decomposition matters because it lets us treat compute efficiency and scaling efficiency as related but distinct optimization problems, each with its own dedicated set of techniques. Both must be addressed to maximize end-to-end MFU.
We tackled these challenges through complementary compute efficiency and scaling efficiency innovations:  
Compute efficiency: Achieved through a customized recommendation kernel library — Jagged Flash Attention (JFA), GDPA, Block-Attention, etc. — and mixed ultra-low precision training (including MXFP8 attention and MLP) optimized for recommendation workloads, purpose-built to leverage the latest generation GPU architecture.
Scaling efficiency: Topology-aware 5D parallelism with Streaming Multiprocessor (SM)-free collectives — 2D FSDP + Expert Parallelism for dense parameters, combined with Fully Sharded 2D Model Parallelism for sparse parameters — co-designed with Meta’s multi-tiered network hierarchy to reduce communication overhead.
The result: We doubled GEM’s E2E training efficiency to 20-25% MFU over the past 12 months while scaling total training FLOPs by 4x. Training a foundation model at the intersection of LLMs and recommendation systems is a co-design problem, not a software problem or a hardware problem alone. This 2x efficiency gain came from carefully considering every layer of the stack for optimization — kernels, precision, parallelism, networking, and memory all had to move together.
For the full technical story, see our companion blog: GEM Training: Train Meta’s LLM-Scale Ads Recommendation Model Efficiently.
The Future of RecSys Foundation Models 
Looking forward, we are excited to extend GEM to learn from all of Meta’s platform data, capturing behavior across organic and ads engagements spanning text, images, and video. We’re building toward LLM-scale long context, giving the model the ability to reason over longer spans of engagement context. This will unlock better ad relevance and help advertisers connect with the right audiences more efficiently.
We will continue to scale GEM on even larger compute clusters, opening new scaling opportunities. We are introducing AI-driven optimizations, such as ecosystem enhancement and architecture co-design, to accelerate future evolutions. These optimizations will iteratively refine model architecture in lockstep with hardware advancements, so that each new generation delivers more intelligence per dollar of compute. We will evolve the post-training paradigm with reasoning capability to transfer more of this intelligence to downstream models, further improving advertiser performance and user experience.

posts.title: OCP Summit 2026: Powering AI with Open Innovations in Scale-Up, Scale-Out, and Scale-Across Networks
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
At the 2026 Open Compute Project Global Summit, Meta is sharing the next generation of open networking infrastructure, including: 

Our first liquid-cooled network rack (IcePack), and 102.4T switch platform (IceCube).
Flattened Planar Fabric (FPF), a multiplane backend scale-out fabric that fundamentally changes how GPUs connect to the network
MetaRoCE, our open-source AI transport protocol.
Launching the Open Switch Platform Architecture (OSPA) initiative within OCP.
We’re inviting engineers, silicon vendors, system integrators, and operators to join us and the OCP community in meeting the challenges of building open, efficient, and sustainable AI infrastructure.
At Meta, we believe that open networking is critical for building high-performance, scalable, and sustainable infrastructure, and we’ve acted on that conviction since co-founding the Open Compute Project (OCP) in 2011. 
Throughout the ongoing AI revolution, Meta has pushed the boundaries of what’s possible in data center networking and shared our advances with the industry. At OCP 2025, we introduced our latest AI scale-out fabrics and drove the creation of the Ethernet for Scale-Up Networking (ESUN) initiative.
This year at OCP 2026, we’re sharing the networking innovations that directly support our latest AI workloads such as Meta’s Muse Wonder and Muse Spark models, and Muse, our personal AI agent built for everyone. Here’s some of what’s new:


The 102.4T scale-out switch: Meta’s first liquid-cooled network rack (IcePack) and 102.4T switch blades (IceCube), designed to support high power density, deliver higher thermal efficiency, and enable gigawatt-scale AI clusters.
The scale-out Flattened Planar Fabric (FPF): Meta’s multiplane fabric, enabling larger, highly efficient GPU clusters with lower latency — with learnings shared with our cloud partners.
Scale-across for multi-site clusters: Meta’s petabit-scale backend aggregation (BAG) super-spine and how large-scale training jobs deal with failures at this scale — with an overview of how we’ve built SRv6 regional backbones using FBOSS and SAI to handle even longer distances
Ethernet for Scale-Up Networking: Meta’s MTIA 300 system uses Tahan, an Ethernet-based 51.2T scale-up switch, delivering 6.4 Tbps per accelerator — with a preview of next-gen 72-accelerator-per-rack design on 102.4T silicon and moving toward an ESUN-based implementation with future chips.
Open Switch Platform Architecture (OSPA): a new OCP initiative, co-led by Meta, Microsoft, and Alibaba, that standardizes the switch platform layer — with specification v1.0 now submitted to OCP.
MetaRoCE: Meta’s RDMA transport protocol for AI networks — now with open-source implementations.
The 102.4T Generation: Liquid-Cooled Networking at AI Scale
As AI clusters grow to gigawatt scale, network switches must deliver dramatically more bandwidth while fitting within increasingly dense power and cooling envelopes. Our answer is the IcePack rack, Meta’s first-generation liquid-cooled network rack.
IcePack is based on OCP’s ORV3-HPRv1 rack standard. IceCube switch blades — 102.4-Tbps fabric switches that deliver 128×800G non-blocking switching capacity — sit inside each rack. IceCube comes in two variants, one built on Broadcom’s Tomahawk6C switch ASIC and one on NVIDIA Spectrum-6 Switch ASIC. Both run Meta’s open-source FBOSS network operating system that leverages OCP SAI (Switch Abstraction Interface). 
This new generation represents a 2x bandwidth increase over our 51.2T platforms while achieving the thermal density required for next-generation AI data centers.
The IcePack rack — Meta’s first liquid-cooled network rack, populated with IceCube 102T switch blades.
IceCube — Meta’s 102.4 Tbps liquid-cooled switch blade, delivering 128×800G non-blocking capacity and running FBOSS.
Scaling AI Fabrics From Building to Region
As seen at Meta and across the industry, AI clusters now span buildings, campuses, and multiple regions. This demands fabric architectures that are not only massive in scale but also resilient and flexible.
Flattened Planar Fabric (FPF): More Resilient, Larger Clusters
We’re introducing Flattened Planar Fabric (FPF), Meta’s multiplane backend scale-out fabric that fundamentally changes how GPUs connect to the network and the network control plane of the fabric.
With FPF, each GPU connects via eight independent 100G links to eight different switches (one per network plane). This multiplane approach replaces the traditional single-plane uplink architecture and delivers four key advantages:
Larger non-blocking GPU clusters compared to single-plane topologies, which enables the scale required for our largest AI training workloads
A flattened topology, moving from the 3-tier Clos fabric of our NSF fabric to a 2-tier Clos fabric. Removing this tier of switches reduces network hops, latency, and infrastructure cost.
NIC-level hardware load balancing: Load balancing, traditionally done by network switches, now starts at the NIC, which sprays every packet across all eight planes in hardware.
A combined control plane for fault tolerance: The control plane of FPF includes both the switches and the hosts, allowing the host to steer traffic away from downed planes. 
Meta collaborated closely with NVIDIA on developing FPF running inside Meta’s infrastructure, leveraging NVIDIA Spectrum-X Multiplane innovations to ensure FPF has high performance even under assorted failure conditions and operational lifecycle scenarios. Going beyond our own infrastructure, Meta and NVIDIA have been working closely with our joint cloud partners to help standardize multiplane fabrics implementations within those partners based on our FPF learnings.
Bridging On-Prem Data Centers and Public Cloud
This work with cloud providers on FPF is just one example of how we at Meta are not just building our own infrastructure, but are helping our partners’ infrastructure. 
Our ambitions for scaling our AI capacity cannot be met by building data centers alone, because construction runs on multi-year lead times while demand moves in months. So we use leased facilities and public cloud capacity, alongside our own campuses, to close the gap. But it only works if the network behaves the same way no matter where the GPUs sit.
That is genuinely difficult, because cloud networking is not the same as owning the rack. Fabric topologies differ from provider to provider rather than following one uniform design. Buffering is often shallower, which changes congestion and loss behavior. RDMA transports are provider-specific, and some clouds still run InfiniBand rather than Ethernet and RoCE. What works for a handful of cloud instances also tends to break at fleet scale.
At OCP we’re sharing how we’re converging these environments into a single operational model. That includes a standardized performance validation framework — cloud partners run a common suite of point-to-point and collective benchmarks, scaling from tens to over a thousand GPUs, before a cluster is ever handed over, so performance is proven rather than assumed. It includes normalizing heterogeneous, often multiplane fabrics, mapping divergent traffic-class schemes and congestion-control parameters onto our lossless RDMA classes so end-to-end paths behave predictably across different vendors’ NICs and switches.
The principle we keep applying is that heterogeneity is manageable but standardization is what makes it affordable. Testing and qualification, RDMA transport and congestion behavior, and telemetry all still diverge across providers, and every divergence becomes engineering work. 
BAG: Scale-Across Aggregation
The scale of AI capacity Meta has committed to this decade — Prometheus at roughly 1 gigawatt in 2026, and Hyperion scaling toward 5 gigawatts— means a single cluster now outgrows any single region. Our backend aggregation (BAG) layer is a centralized, Ethernet-based super-spine that interconnects many spine-layer fabrics into one mega cluster spanning buildings, campuses, and regions. It operates at petabit scale — inter-BAG capacity between a pair of regions reaches tens of petabits per second. BAG is what allows Prometheus to function as a single cluster even though its capacity is spread across conventional data center buildings, weatherproof outdoor structures, and adjacent colocation space.
At this reach, distance itself becomes a design constraint. Lossless Ethernet requires buffer headroom proportional to cable length, so once links stretch tens of kilometers, buffer management turns into a first-order problem rather than a tuning detail. And getting it wrong risks congestion spreading well beyond the link that caused it. Instead of provisioning every link for a worst-case distance, FBOSS now measures actual cable length in place, timing probe traffic on an uncongested queue to derive round-trip distance, and allocates headroom against the measurement.
Load balancing also has to reason about paths that are degraded rather than simply down. BAG uses eBGP link-bandwidth signaling so traffic is distributed in proportion to the capacity actually available on each path, with deliberate damping so that a single link failure does not ripple routing churn across the domain. And because inter-fabric latency is several times intra-fabric latency, collective communication libraries — which generally choose algorithms without any awareness of network distance — can fall off a performance cliff. 
We’ve been addressing that from both directions, with adaptive routing improvements to reduce the latency penalty and scheduling that minimizes how much collective traffic needs to cross the BAG layer at all. Training remains resilient throughout. When a replica fails, it is automatically excluded and the surviving replicas continue synchronizing across BAG.
The direction of travel is longer distances still — training jobs spanning regions tens, hundreds, or thousands of kilometers apart — and increasingly heterogeneous clusters that mix hardware generations and vendors.
Backend aggregation (BAG) connects building-scale AI fabrics — both DSF and NSF — across sub-regions into a unified training network.
SRv6-Powered Regional Backbone Using FBOSS
We’ve deployed Segment Routing over IPv6 (SRv6) using FBOSS for our regional backbone networks. This enables more flexible traffic engineering and simplified operations as we interconnect AI clusters across geographies — running on open shallow-buffer switch platforms powered by Cisco SiliconOne, with ongoing work to onboard additional silicon families, all managed under FBOSS using OCP SAI.
Meta’s Regional Backbone (RBB) interconnects data center campuses and bridges to public cloud capacity.
Ethernet for Scale-Up: Our Commitment to Ethernet
A defining milestone of OCP 2026 is proving that Ethernet can serve the scale-up domain — the high-bandwidth, ultra-low-latency interconnects between accelerators within a rack or pod that have traditionally required proprietary technologies.
Tahan: Ethernet-Based Scale-Up Switch
We’re introducing Tahan, Meta’s Ethernet-based scale-up switch — purpose-built for our MTIA 300 training accelerators. Tahan is built on the 51.2 Tbps Tomahawk 5 ASIC from Broadcom, offering total capacity of 64x800G, half of which is used to provide scale-up connectivity to the accelerators via the backplane. Four Tahan switches interconnect 16 accelerators in a non-blocking topology.
Importantly, Tahan reuses the same lossless RoCE transport (routed IPv6, PFC, AI-tuned QoS) as our scale-out network, unifying both scale-up and scale-out fabrics under FBOSS.
Tahan, Meta’s first open, Ethernet-based scale-up switch (32×800G), liquid-cooled and running FBOSS.
Next-Generation Scale-Up: 72 Accelerators per Rack on 102.4T Silicon
We’re also previewing the next-generation scale-up blade, a 216×400G switch built on 102.4 Tbps Broadcom Tomahawk6C silicon. Eight of these switches interconnect 72 accelerators per rack, a dramatic increase in density enabled by the bandwidth of the 102.4T generation. A future generation of this scale-up blade is planned to adopt OCP Ethernet for Scale-Up Networking (ESUN) as the scale-up data plane, cementing our commitment to open standards for the entire scale-up stack.
The next-generation MTIA scale-up blade: 216×400G on 102.4 Tbps silicon, adopting OCP ESUN as the scale-up data plane.
ESUN Evolving
The ESUN initiative we founded within OCP last year has made significant progress. Working alongside AMD, Arista, ARM, Broadcom, Cisco, HPE, Marvell, Microsoft, and NVIDIA, ESUN is advancing open specifications for:


Protocol headers and framing optimized for scale-up topologies.
Error handling mechanisms for lossless multi-hop fabrics.
Alignment with UEC and IEEE standards.
This work has already produced a concrete result with the ESUN 1.0 Network Operator Requirements Base Specification released earlier this year. ESUN 1.0 deliberately focuses on the fabric, defining what the network must deliver while leaving implementation flexibility to GPU and accelerator vendors, which broadens adoption. It also coordinates with existing standards bodies, leveraging work underway in IEEE and the Ultra Ethernet Consortium (UEC) rather than duplicating it.
Since publishing ESUN 1.0, the group is now close to the next version, ESUN 1.1, tackling new features such as switch profiles and inter-packet gap reduction that further optimize Ethernet for low-latency, scale-up use cases.
ESUN’s technical focus: a fabric-centric scope that preserves GPU implementation flexibility, coordinated with IEEE and UEC standards work with the ESUN 1.0 specification already released.
With Tahan shipping today, a 72-accelerator-per-rack design on the horizon adopting ESUN as its data plane, and ESUN continuing to evolve its open specifications, we’re helping build a complete open platform for the scale-up future.
Ecosystem Enablement and Open Transport
Our commitment to openness extends across the full networking stack — from switch platform hardware to transport protocols.
OSPA: Open Switch Platform Architecture
SAI made switch data plane software portable across silicon. But the layer beneath it, the switch platform layer, has remained proprietary and fragmented. Every new hardware platform requires months of duplicated, custom engineering to bring up, and a lack of standard platform design multiplies long-term maintenance and troubleshooting cost. In an era of compressed AI hardware cycles, that onboarding tax has become untenable.
To fix this, we’re co-leading a new OCP initiative with Microsoft and Alibaba, the Open Switch Platform Architecture (OSPA) — a unified reference design for the switch platform layer. 
OSPA standardizes the hardware and software interfaces for:


Power management and power sequencing.
Sensor and environment control, including thermal and fan management.
Hardware inventory management and device enumeration.
Out-of-band hardware interfaces (management Ethernet, serial console, USB, LED indicators).
Firmware maintenance and updates.
Platform troubleshooting and diagnostics.
FBOSS Ecosystem Enablement

Over the past year we made a major push to extend open-source FBOSS so that switch vendors can self-onboard their own platforms without Meta engineers in the loop for the port. The goal is a self-service model in which multiple new switch platforms can be developed concurrently, giving vendors access to a hyperscale-proven NOS as they build FBOSS-compatible hardware.
Vendors and developers can get started at the FBOSS documentation site and the FBOSS GitHub repository.
MetaRoCE: Open-Source Transport for AI Clusters
As we recently announced, MetaRoCE is our open-source RDMA transport protocol optimized for AI cluster networks over Ethernet. MetaRoCE provides the congestion control and reliability semantics that distributed AI training workloads demand. It’s purpose-built for the unique traffic patterns of collective communication across large-scale Ethernet fabrics. 
At OCP, we are announcing our open-source MetaRoCE implementations, enabling the broader AI infrastructure community to adopt and build upon a production-proven transport stack.
Join Us in Building the Open Future of AI Networking
The pace of AI infrastructure evolution continues to accelerate. The challenges of building open, efficient, and sustainable AI networking are too large for any single company to solve alone.
We invite engineers, silicon vendors, system integrators, and operators to join us and the OCP community in defining what comes next. Visit our presentations at OCP 2026, explore our open-source contributions including FBOSS and MetaRoCE, and collaborate with us on building the networking infrastructure the AI era demands.
The authors are members of the Network Infrastructure team at Meta.
