posts.title: Netflix Stratum Media Processing: Automated Container Right-Sizing
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
By Violetta Pidvolotska and Naveen Mareddy
Stratum is Netflix’s internal serverless media processing platform, shaped by over a decade of experience developing large-scale distributed systems. It powers a wide range of media workloads — including encoding, packaging, inspection, and quality scoring — behind playback, advertising, studio workflows, AI embeddings, and more.
Engineers develop Stratum functions by packaging application code and OS dependencies into OCI images. Stratum then schedules these containers as batch jobs on Netflix’s Titus compute platform, with upstream services triggering function executions.
Every day, Stratum manages hundreds of thousands of containers across bursty, high-throughput, and latency-sensitive workloads. As Netflix’s core media processing platform, this load needs to scale as new content formats enter the catalog, such as podcasts, live events, sports, ads, or regional ingests like TF1 in France.
To request resources for these functions, owners specify their CPU, memory, disk, and network limits as YAML configuration, as shown below:
functionName: VideoEncoder.encodeV1
resources:
  numCpus: 8
  memoryInMB: 18000
  diskSizeInMB: 50000
  networkInMbps: 1000
Maintaining optimal values manually is challenging amidst evolving Netflix infrastructure, EC2 instance upgrades, and application-level changes. Consequently, configs are often over-provisioned upfront or slowly drift away from their ideal values over time. Mis-sized configurations are a universal pain of large-scale serverless platforms, causing additional cognitive load for function builders and operational costs for platform owners.
In this post, we share how we built the Stratum Resource Tuner (SRT) — an automated system that safely right-sizes running containers in production without human intervention. We will walk through real-world examples, our safety architecture, and what we learned when an automated change went wrong.
The Challenge: Over-Provisioning
When engineers write a new Stratum function, they typically copy a resource YAML from an existing function or size it for the absolute worst-case scenario. Once running in production, engineers rarely revisit these configurations until a failure occurs, prompting them to over-provision resources out of an abundance of caution.
Manual resource tuning does not scale for the following reasons:

High Operational Friction: Downsizing requires days of manual metric monitoring and trial-and-error testing, diverting valuable engineering cycles away from other high-impact work. If a cut goes too far, engineers face production incidents — making manual tuning a high-risk, low-reward task.
Continuous Infrastructure & Codec Evolution: Cloud providers regularly upgrade their hardware. A resource allocation that was optimal on an older hardware generation quietly becomes inefficient on newer hardware. At the same time, Netflix continuously advances media standards and improves encoding algorithms (such as AV1, AV2, and spatial audio). An allocation tuned for one codec might not be optimal when an improved algorithm is released.
Dynamic Workload Evolution: As Netflix expands into new media types — such as streaming video podcasts, sports, interactive AI-adapted ad formats, and major broadcaster integrations like TF1 in France — media processing footprints can change unpredictably, rendering static container resource limits imprecise.
Rising Industry Hardware Costs: Driven by massive global AI infrastructure demand, server hardware and DRAM prices continue to climb, making idle container memory significantly more expensive to waste.
Compounding Platform Scale: At Netflix scale, even minor over-provisioning multiplies exponentially across hundreds of thousands of daily container executions, compounding wasted capacity across the entire Stratum platform.

To understand the scale of the challenge, we analyzed historical usage across Stratum’s workloads. The telemetry confirmed our hypothesis: over-provisioning was frequent, wasted compute was compounding, and the sustainable path forward required a fundamental re-evaluation of how resource configurations are managed.
Meet the Stratum Resource Tuner
To address the challenges listed above, we built the Stratum Resource Tuner (SRT) to automatically right-size Stratum containers. Our north star is to ensure that users never have to manually specify the resource configurations. We started with a handful of high-throughput workloads with relaxed latency requirements, which account for the majority (70%–80%) of resource usage.
As a quick note on terminology, we use “right-sizing” and “tuning” interchangeably in this post. “Downsizing” means decreasing resource limits, while “upsizing” means increasing them. Since our goal is to optimize for cost, this post focuses on downsizing.
Automatic right-sizing is not enabled by default. Function owners must manually opt in on a per resource type basis (e.g., CPU, memory, network, or disk). Once enrolled, SRT operates without a human in the loop across five steps:
Figure 1: SRT Workflow High-Level
Collect resource usage metrics across all executions of that function.
Generate a recommendation for each resource type (e.g., CPU or memory).
Verify the recommendation through experiments.
Apply or reject the recommendation based on the results of experiments.
Monitor post-apply metrics, watching for anomalies after applying the recommendation.

“Recommendation” is a key construct in SRT and serves as the primary unit of operation. As SRT executes its steps, it promotes the recommendation through several stages:
Figure 2: Recommendation State Machine
CREATED: A scheduled workflow generated the recommendation.
EVALUATING: Recommendation verification is running, and SRT is analyzing the results.
APPLIED: All experiments passed, and SRT automatically rolled out the recommended configuration.
REJECTED: At least one experiment failed, leaving the function configuration untouched.
MONITORED: SRT monitors the recommendation during a post-apply soak period to verify stability.

The sections below examine each of these stages in detail. To illustrate the flow, we will follow the real-world lifecycle of the VideoEncoder.encodeV1 function — a high-throughput video encoding function whose over-provisioned memory and CPU footprints were successfully tuned.
Note that all operational thresholds and safety limits discussed below are fully configurable per function to accommodate varying workload characteristics and risk tolerances.
Metrics Collection
To make these recommendations possible, we need a solid metrics collection mechanism. Every Stratum container reports its function execution metadata, infrastructure dimensions, and resource utilization (CPU, memory, disk, and network) at sub-minute resolution.
These metrics flow through Keystone, Netflix’s real-time event streaming platform, and land in two separate datastores:
Figure 3: Metrics Collection
Execution summaries store: Stores execution-level summary metrics indexed in Elasticsearch for fast point lookups, serving as our short-term datastore for querying and inspecting individual runs.
High-resolution long-term store: Stores raw, high-resolution usage metrics in Iceberg tables. While slower to query, it serves as our long-term datastore, holding months of history for resource utilization trend analysis.

One record is written per execution, which is represented as a span. Here is how these records look for a single span of our VideoEncoder.encodeV1 function.
In Elasticsearch, the record captures the high-level summary of the completed span, identified by tags.stratum.spanId:
{
  "tags.stratum.spanId": "38536313f65f060a",
  "tags.functionName": "VideoEncoder.encodeV1",
  "tags.stratum.phase": "run",
  "tags.stratum.success": true,
  "tags.stratum.retriedWithMoreResources": false,
  "tags.stratum.function.execDurationSecs": 26,
  "tags.cpuCount": 8,
  "tags.memoryInMB": 18000,
  "tags.diskInMB": 50000,
  "tags.networkInMbps": 1000,
  "tags.titusTaskId": "06e1a7c0-2502-4a54-905f-b13a1e786107",
  "tags.instanceType": "r7a.24xlarge",
  "tags.nf.region": "us-east-1",
  "ts": 1780743028000
}
In Iceberg, the record contains the same metadata, but adds the sub-minute resource utilization timeseries tracked during that span:
{
  "span_id": "38536313f65f060a",
  "function_name": "VideoEncoder.encodeV1",
  "phase": "run",
  "success": true,
  "start_epoch_secs": 1780743002,
  "end_epoch_secs": 1780743028,
  "runtime_secs": 26,
  "cpu_requested": 8,
  "memory_mb_requested": 18000,
  "disk_mb_requested": 50000,
  "network_mbps_requested": 1000,
  "titusTaskId": "06e1a7c0-2502-4a54-905f-b13a1e786107",
  "instance_type": "r7a.24xlarge",
  "tags.stratum.retriedWithMoreResources": false,
  "env": "prod",
  "resource_usage": [ 
   { "cpu_usage": 1.13, "memory_mb": 3701.37, "disk_mb": 20120.4, "net_in_mb": 221.09, "net_out_mb": 0.12 },
   { "cpu_usage": 2.25, "memory_mb": 3584.09, "disk_mb": 25410.1, "net_in_mb": 0.02, "net_out_mb": 0.05 },
   { "cpu_usage": 4.16, "memory_mb": 6750.79, "disk_mb": 30400.5, "net_in_mb": 165.90, "net_out_mb": 0.38 },
   ... 
  ]
}
Recommendation Generation
A scheduled Conductor workflow runs daily, reading the past month of usage data from Iceberg and generating recommendations for every function and resource type. The workflow also generates recommendations for functions that have not opted into automatic right-sizing to preview potential savings.
Each recommendation is saved in the recommendations datastore, enabling us to query and filter recommendations by function, resource type, or status on an ad hoc basis.
Figure 4: Recommendation Generation Sequence
For each function and resource type, the workflow applies the following generation logic:

Filter by workload type: We only tune high-throughput workloads. This focuses our efforts on right-sizing, which yields the most meaningful fleet-wide savings.
Aggressively tune CPU and network: We target p99 usage with no extra headroom. CPU and network are compressible resources; if a container occasionally hits these limits, the function might execute slightly slower.
Conservatively tune memory and disk: We target p99.9 usage and include a safety buffer. Running out of physical memory or disk space causes hard failures — such as Out of Memory (OOM) or Out of Disk (OOD) crashes — making a protective margin essential.
Apply safeguards to changes: We discard recommendations if the absolute reduction is too small to justify operational effort. For memory and disk, we clamp the maximum reduction allowed in a single cycle to 15% — a safety limit introduced after learning from early production runs.

The workflow creates new recommendations in the CREATED state. If a recommendation already exists in this state for a given function and resource type, SRT overwrites it with updated calculations. Once a recommendation advances past the CREATED state, its recommended_value and stats fields become immutable. Subsequent daily runs generate a new recommendation with a unique ID instead of modifying the existing record.
Here is how these recommendations look across resource types in their initial CREATED state for our VideoEncoder.encodeV1 function:

CPU recommendation

{
  "function_name": "VideoEncoder.encodeV1",
  "env": "prod", "resource_type": "CPU",
  "current_value": 8, "recommended_value": 4,
  "status": "CREATED",
  "resource_cost_usd_per_hour": ***,
  "stats": {
    "usage": { "p99": 4.16, "p999": 4.57 },
    "execution": {
      "total_fn_executions": 748762182,
      "success_fn_executions_pct": 99.75,
      "total_fn_exec_runtime_hr": 88102723
    },
    "window": { "start": "2026-05-05T00:00:00Z", "end": "2026-06-05T00:00:00Z" }
  },
  "experiment_inputs": null,
  "experiment_workflow_execution_id": null,
  "outcome_message": null,
  "finalized_at": null
}
Memory recommendation (15% reduction in one step)

{  "id": "2edb734a-6184-4f5e-8ffa-23004bd665d7",
  "function_name": "VideoEncoder.encodeV1",
  "env": "prod", "resource_type": "MEMORY_MB",
  "current_value": 18000, "recommended_value": 15300,
  "status": "CREATED",
  "resource_cost_usd_per_hour": ***,
  "stats": {
    "usage": { "avg": 5296.43, "p99": 6750.8, "p999": 7820.3 },
    "execution": {
      "total_fn_executions": 748762182,
      "success_fn_executions_pct": 99.75,
      "total_fn_exec_runtime_hr": 88102723
    },
    "window": { "start": "2026-05-05T00:00:00Z", "end": "2026-06-05T00:00:00Z" }
  },
  "experiment_inputs": null,
  "experiment_workflow_execution_id": null,
  "outcome_message": null,
  "finalized_at": null
}
As the recommendation moves through its lifecycle, SRT populates the remaining parameters.
When proceeding to the verification stage, SRT transitions the recommendation status to EVALUATING, records the target experiment settings, and links the active workflow execution tracking the experiment.
Finally, once verification runs complete, the status changes to APPLIED or REJECTED, storing the outcome details and completion timestamp for analysis.
Retry with More Resources
We take a conservative approach to generating recommendations, prioritizing system stability over extreme efficiency. Because recommendations rely on historical usage data, they cannot always anticipate sudden spikes or novel workload profiles when functions encounter heavy, unseen requests.
To handle these unexpected spikes, we developed a fail-safe mechanism. A watcher process running in each tuned container tracks memory and disk usage during function execution. If the container exceeds the pre-set thresholds, 85% for non-cached memory usage or 95% for disk usage, the watcher flags the execution as high risk, cancels execution, and re-queues the task onto a larger container:
new_container_size = original_container_size * 1.5
This 1.5 multiplier only applies to memory and disk dimensions.
Figure 5: Retry with More Resources
This “retry with more resources” mechanism serves as our safety net: larger container configurations are applied only when retrying tasks to self-heal from edge cases. Although these infrequent retries incur additional compute costs and latency, they allow us to keep day-to-day configurations highly optimized without having to size for rare, costly outliers up front.
For our VideoEncoder.encodeV1 function, if a heavy run causes memory usage to exceed the 85% threshold (15,300 MB) within its current 18,000 MB container, the system aborts the execution and reruns it on a 27,000 MB container.
While we prefer to trigger retries based on actual OOM or OOD events rather than pre-set thresholds, technical constraints in our current architecture make true event detection challenging. Using pre-set thresholds serves as a reliable stopgap while we develop improved detection capabilities.
SRT automatically enables the retry mechanism for any function opted into memory or disk right-sizing. Each Stratum container reports retry events, which flow into Elasticsearch and Iceberg alongside standard performance telemetry.
Recommendation Verification
Every recommendation must pass a two-stage verification process managed by a Conductor workflow before rollout. During this EVALUATING stage, SRT executes two distinct experiment types:

Synthetic experiment: A low-cost, low-risk test to catch obvious regressions before production rollout.
Production experiment: A live evaluation that validates changes across diverse production workloads to increase confidence.

A recommendation advances to production testing only after passing the synthetic experiment. When an opted-in function has multiple pending recommendations, SRT prioritizes and evaluates the candidates with the highest estimated savings first.
Figure 6: Evaluating Stage
Synthetic experiment:

Runs in a test environment isolated from production traffic.
Sets up two clusters: one for the current and one for the recommended config.
Replays identical request sets across both clusters simultaneously without splitting traffic, exposing both configurations to 100% of test requests.
Typically runs for 1–2 hours.
Runs to completion without early termination checks.
Figure 7: Synthetic Experiment Flow
Production experiment:

Runs in production on real user traffic, split three ways:
◦ ~90% remains on the main cluster (current production config).
◦ ~5% goes to a baseline cluster (current production config).
◦ ~5% goes to an experimental cluster (recommendation config).
Evaluates recommendations against a similarly sized baseline cluster rather than the main cluster to preserve comparable traffic profiles.
Typically runs from one day to one week, depending on traffic volume.
Fails fast: cancels the experiment early if regressions are detected.
Figure 8: Production Experiment Flow
The Stratum platform executes other experiments alongside SRT experiments. To avoid over-splitting traffic, SRT experiments run at lower priority and yield resources to active, higher-priority experiments.
Traffic arrives in irregular bursts separated by multi-day or multi-week lulls. The verification pipeline accommodates these variable arrival patterns rather than expecting steady traffic.
Back to our VideoEncoder.encodeV1 memory recommendation (18,000 MB → 15,300 MB), verification is triggered with:
{
  "recommendationId": "2edb734a-6184-4f5e-8ffa-23004bd665d7",
  "syntheticExperiment": { "numberOfExecutions": 3000 },
  "productionExperiment": {
    "enabled": true,
    "maxContainers": 20, // max containers shift to baseline & experimental clusters
    "upGateTimeoutMinutes": 10080, // time to wait for traffic to start flowing
    "maxRunDurationMinutes": 1240, // max time to run the experiment once traffic starts
    "minSamples": 500 // min executions needed on both clusters before evaluating
  }
}
Both verification stages evaluate recommendations against two sequential checks, terminating immediately if either fails:

Retries with more resources: Restricts memory and disk downsizes to a maximum 1% retry threshold over the experiment duration.
Execution time: Compares median runtimes to prevent outlier distortion, permitting up to a 10–15% slowdown relative to baseline, depending on workload, and is configurable by function.

If a recommendation passes both verification stages, SRT updates its status to APPLIED and rolls out the configuration to the main production cluster. If a check fails at any point, SRT marks the recommendation as REJECTED and preserves the existing configuration. SRT sends notifications for both outcomes.
For VideoEncoder.encodeV1, both stages passed cleanly:
{
  "outcome": "APPLIED",
  "syntheticExperiment": {
    "result": "SUCCESS",
    "samples": { "baseline": 3000, "experimental": 3000 },
    "medianExecutionSecs": { "baseline": 59.0, "experimental": 59.0 },
    "slownessIncreasePct": 0.0,
    "retryRatePct": { "baseline": 0.0, "experimental": 0.0 }
  },
  "productionExperiment": {
    "result": "SUCCESS",
    "samples": { "baseline": 50361, "experimental": 49790 },
    "medianExecutionSecs": { "baseline": 196.0, "experimental": 198.0 },
    "slownessIncreasePct": 1.0,
    "retryRatePct": { "baseline": 0.0, "experimental": 0.0 }
  }
}
The recommendation moved to the APPLIED state, permanently setting the memory allocation for VideoEncoder.encodeV1 to 15,300 MB. We observed similarly clean results for the CPU recommendation, which reduced CPU allocation from 8 cores to 4.
Post-Apply Monitoring
Passing verification experiments does not mark the end of the recommendation lifecycle. Updated function code, modified input parameters, or underlying changes in the compute environment (Titus/EC2) can alter production behavior over time. To ensure configuration safety and foster feature adoption, we instituted continuous post-apply monitoring for applied changes.
We monitor metrics for 90 days across two rolling time windows: a 30-minute fast window and a 24-hour slow window. Each window maintains specific alert thresholds: a 3% retry rate over 30 minutes or a 2% rate over 24 hours triggers an automated notification.
At steady state, workloads exhibit baseline retry rates around 0.1%, with rates up to 2%–3% falling within acceptable operational variances. Most applied recommendations remained stable over the past three months.
VideoEncoder.encodeV1 has operated on its tuned configuration for months without breaching thresholds. However, VideoEncoder.encodeV2 presented a challenging edge case: a 50% memory reduction passed all verification checks and ran stably for two weeks before an unexpected traffic shift drove retry rates above 60%.
Figure 9: Unexpected Retries Spike
Because early versions lacked automated rollback capabilities, engineers manually triaged exception cases. This incident highlighted the need for automated mitigation, prompting us to construct self-healing rollback functionality.
Today, the two auto-revert windows look like this:

Last 30 minutes: 3% retries warn us; 10% triggers an auto-revert.
Last 24 hours: A 2% retry rate triggers both an alert and an automatic revert.

Breaching an auto-revert threshold immediately restores the function configuration to its pre-recommendation baseline.
Figure 10: Recommendation Auto-Revert
We intentionally maintain straightforward revert logic — restoring the last known stable configuration rather than attempting dynamic resource adjustments during an incident.
The VideoEncoder.encodeV2 incident also reshaped our recommendation generation rules for memory and disk allocations. Rather than applying full target reductions immediately, SRT now applies smaller, incremental 15% step changes, advancing only after confirming stability at each step. Additionally, we introduced a global kill switch to disable automated right-sizing across all functions in case of unexpected issues or side effects.
Additionally, we enforce a mandatory cooldown period — typically one week — before initiating new experiments on a function. Pausing adjustments allows us to observe performance across diverse production traffic patterns, identifying potential risks before applying subsequent recommendations.
Where Are We Today
Oversized containers and config drift don’t have to be an accepted tax of running serverless workloads at scale. By building the Stratum Resource Tuner, we transformed manual, risk-averse resource sizing into an automated, self-healing pipeline. Through real-world workloads and hard lessons from unexpected spikes, we’ve proven that continuous right-sizing can safely deliver significant gains in infrastructure efficiency.
We initially focused on right-sizing high-throughput video encoding workloads, aiming for an initial 5% reduction in overall Stratum compute costs. For instance, VideoEncoder.encodeV1 achieved a 50% reduction in CPU usage and 40% in memory usage without compromising performance or retry rates.
However, edge cases like VideoEncoder.encodeV2 highlighted key lessons: large single-step reductions can introduce hidden risks, and manual incident response slows recovery. These insights led us to enforce stricter safety guardrails in the Stratum Resource Tuner, including capping memory and disk reductions at 15% per cycle and adding automated rollbacks when retry thresholds are breached. Guided by these safeguards, re-tuning VideoEncoder.encodeV2 yielded a stable 20% memory reduction with zero subsequent incidents.
Looking ahead, our key priorities include:

Expand SRT beyond high-throughput encoding workloads to support a wider variety of functions and workload types.
Further tune the resources in regions with constrained resource availability.
Move from reactive alerts to proactive, automated upsizing for under-provisioned functions.
Experiment with intentional upsizing for latency-sensitive workloads to evaluate performance gains and reduce function execution time.
Upgrade our failure signals for OOM/OOD events from lagging indicators to leading indicators to improve tuning precision.

If solving problems like this sounds exciting, we are hiring in our Warsaw office. Check out open roles here.
Credits
Special thanks to Olof Johansson, Jakub Karczewski, Adam Mazur, Ethan Mathieu, Rosanna Lee, Ameya Vasani, Jean Barkhuysen, Paul Hieromnimon, and Adithya Prakash.

posts.title: Can you bake Maven into a neural network?
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
We tried, and it builds. We compiled the decision-making part of a Maven-style build tool into a fixed weight matrix and used it to build a real Java library. The output matches Apache Maven's byte for byte. A clean build with tests took 1.49× as long as the same logic written in Python (95% interval 1.4× to 1.54×, 30 paired runs).
The network’s weight table, one bar per row. Bar height is how often a row ran during one ZXing build; the bright point replays real stretches of that build, one step at a time.



Every Java developer has watched Maven think. It resolves, compiles, tests and packages. Most of that time belongs to javac and JUnit, but threaded through it is a small, fussy piece of logic that decides what happens next. Which version of a library wins when two modules disagree. Which files go to the compiler, and with which flags. Whether a failing test stops the build.
We wanted to know if that piece could live inside a neural network. Not a model trained to guess what Maven usually does next: that kind of model is right most of the time, and a build tool that is right most of the time is broken. We wanted the decision logic itself, compiled into weights, so the network gets the answer exactly right or refuses to answer.
The video at the top of this post is that network. Each of its 26,626 bars is one row of its weight table (model nmvn-exact-v2, explained in the section on making it cheaper), bar height is how often that row ran during one ZXing build, and the bright point replays real stretches of that build, one step at a time. Everything that decides how the build goes is in there.
From a program to a weight table
The trick comes from Handwired: you can write a program and then set a network’s weights so the network is that program. We wrote a small Maven-compatible build controller in a restricted subset of Python and compiled it into a table of 29,625 × 7 numbers, plus 7,382 cells of constants (that’s the first version, v1; a later section shrinks the table to the 26,626 rows you see above). No training, no gradient descent: zero optimizer steps.
Running it is a loop. Each step, the network looks up one row of its table with two matrix multiplications, does the arithmetic that row encodes on a small register file, and writes the result back to memory. The network can’t open files or start javac. When it needs to, it writes a request into a fixed slot in its memory, and a thin bridge carries the request out and writes back the raw answer. The bridge never decides anything. Every choice comes out of the weights.
 div{background:var(--jb-nmvn-soft);border:1px solid var(--jb-nmvn-line);border-radius:12px;padding:16px 18px}

pom.xml bytes+ results so far

Fixed weight tableone row per step,two matmuls to fetch it,no training

A request“read this file”“run javac with…”

Bridgedisk, javac, JUnit,bnd, zip
raw result written back into the network’s memory, and the loop continues

The test subject was ZXing 3.5.3, the barcode library: its parent project and the core and javase modules, built with clean package and the tests on.
Does it actually build?
Yes. The JARs it produced match Apache Maven’s byte for byte, built inside a sandbox where Maven can’t run, the network is off, and neither the Python version of the logic nor Maven’s own outputs can be read. All 549 upstream tests ran and passed, and the freshly built JARs encoded and decoded QR codes correctly in 27 of 27 checks.
519hand-written build cases passed, each checked against real Maven
10,000generated project cases passed
33other small projects built correctly with the same weights
4,796,191network steps for one full ZXing build




Two checks convinced us the work really happens in the weights. The CPU and GPU versions of the network made exactly the same 1,731 requests, in the same order, for a full build. And when we deleted or corrupted the weight file, no build happened at all.
A QR code written by the freshly built ZXing JARs and read back by them.



Watch it build
Left: the controller as ordinary Python. Right: the same controller as a neural network. Both build ZXing for real, one after the other on the same Mac, played back at real speed.
One recorded build on each side, played back in real time. Grey on the timelines is time spent in javac, JUnit, bnd and zip.



The bill
It’s slower, in every scenario we measured. Python runs the controller’s logic directly; the network spends a full round of matrix arithmetic on every tiny instruction, and one ZXing build costs it 4,796,191 of them.

What was timedClassic PythonNeural, CPUNeural, GPU (Metal)Apache Maven 3.9.11Neural CPU / Python

Decisions only (no Java work)146.54 ms4.15 s27.97 s–28.3×
Cold start to first decisions385.94 ms4.80 s28.25 s–12.4×
Clean build with tests15.52 s23.12 s70.11 s15.29 s1.49×
Build that stops at a compile error1.74 s4.41 s22.19 s2.81 s2.53×

Median wall time (lower is better). Last column: neural CPU time divided by Python time.



Clean build with tests, median secondsBar = median; whisker = p25 to p75.Classic Python

15.52 s (n=30)Neural, CPU

23.12 s (n=30)Neural, GPU (Metal)

70.11 s (n=30)Apache Maven 3.9.11

15.29 s (n=30)Clean build with tests, median seconds. Bar = median; whisker = p25 to p75.



On decisions alone the network is far behind. In a whole build the gap shrinks to about one and a half times, because most of the time goes to javac and JUnit and both versions use the same ones. Running the network on the GPU made things worse, not better. A program that executes one instruction after another gives a GPU nothing to do in parallel.

So this is not a faster build tool. It’s a build tool you can hold as a tensor.




Making it cheaper without touching the network
The time is roughly steps × cost per step, so we counted where the steps go. We replayed a full ZXing build in an instruction-level simulator and tallied every instruction it executed. Of v1’s 4,796,191 steps, 652,773 (14%) just copied a value from one register to another, and 553,333 more (12%) loaded a constant or jumped back to the top of a loop. That’s compiler glue, not build logic.
So we left the network alone and fixed the compiler. Results now land directly in the register that needs them, constants ride inside the instruction that uses them, conditions compile straight to branches, and loops test at the bottom instead of jumping back to the top. The machine, its step graph and the GPU kernel are unchanged. Only the table of numbers is different, and smaller.
23%fewer network steps for a full ZXing build (4,796,191 → 3,676,728)
10%fewer rows in the weight table (29,625 → 26,626)
identicaldecisions: fed v1’s recorded inputs, v2 makes the same 1,731 requests in the same order, on CPU and GPU
2 of 2correctness gates re-passed by v2 (same suites, sandboxed build, byte-identical JARs)




Network steps per instruction class, v1 vs v2For the same full ZXing build: v1 ran 4,796,191 steps, v2 ran 3,676,728.v1: 4,796,191 stepsv2: 3,676,728 stepsregister copies0.65M → 0.09M -86%constant loads0.34M → 0.18M -46%unconditional jumps0.22M → 0.04M -81%branches0.70M → 0.66M -6%arithmetic and compares1.42M → 1.24M -13%memory loads and stores1.22M → 1.22M +0%calls and returns0.18M → 0.18M +0%vector ops and I/O0.06M → 0.06M +0%Every step of one full ZXing build, by instruction class (instruction-set simulator replaying the recorded build; the action sequence is identical for both models).





What was timedNeural CPU, v1Neural CPU, v2Python (v2 run)v1 / Pythonv2 / Python (95% CI)

Decisions only (no Java work)4.15 s3.40 s140.81 ms28.3×24.2× (23.6× to 25.2×)
Cold start to first decisions4.80 s4.14 s402.38 ms12.4×10.3× (10.1× to 10.7×)
Clean build with tests23.12 s21.09 s14.83 s1.49×1.42× (1.40× to 1.43×)
Build that stops at a compile error4.41 s3.70 s1.78 s2.53×2.08× (2.05× to 2.11×)

Neural CPU, v1 vs v2 (median wall time). Ratios are neural time / Python time from paired runs in the same session; v1 from nmvn-bench-v0, v2 from the follow-up protocol.



The GPU gains more, because it pays almost purely per step: decisions only took 27.97 s with v1 and 21.61 s with v2 (23% less), close to the cut in steps. It is still the slowest engine.
We re-ran the whole correctness chain on the new weights: every test suite, the sandboxed build that has to produce byte-identical JARs, the negative controls and the CPU/GPU replay. The cut is real but modest where it counts. Java tooling still owns most of a full build, so trimming the network’s share moves the end-to-end number less than the step count suggests.
It isn’t only Maven
To check the compiler isn’t secretly tuned to one program, we gave it something unrelated: a maze solver (breadth-first search, programs/maze/maze_nml.py). It compiled to 279 rows of weights. A small app starts the classic and the neural version at the same moment, as separate processes, and draws each cell as soon as that program reports it.
Recording of the app window, which saves its own frames as it runs;, neural side on CPU. The GPU version takes longer.



On 3 different 171×121 mazes, plain Python, the Python debug shim, the neural CPU run and the neural GPU run produced identical event sequences: every visited cell, in the same order, with the same distances. The first maze took 2,572,288 network steps. Neural on CPU took 161× to 168× as long as plain Python, and on GPU 791× to 812× (each program’s own timer, one run per maze, so treat these as rough).
So it’s slower. Is it even useful?
Fair question. We asked it too. If you want a faster build, no: keep using Maven. And a bigger GPU won’t rescue it, because the network runs one instruction at a time and nothing in a build controller can be spread across thousands of cores.
Speed was never the interesting part, though. What we ended up with is a neural network where every weight has a known meaning, and that is rare. Here’s where we think it’s worth something, most convinced first.
An answer key for people who take networks apart
Interpretability research tries to work out what a network does from its weights alone. The hard part is grading the answer, because for a trained model nobody knows the truth. This network ships with the truth. Apart from a seven-row start-up stub, every one of its 26,626 rows belongs to a known function among the controller’s 249, and we know what each of those functions does. So we can point at the rows of do_surefire, the part that runs the tests and decides whether a failure stops the build. If a tool claims to have found “the dependency-resolution circuit”, you can check it. Hand-built test networks tend to be small toys. This one does a real job on a real codebase, and we think that’s its best use.
Exact parts inside models that guess
A model that picks the right library version 99% of the time is wrong once every hundred builds. Compiled weights are a way to put an exact subroutine in the same form as a learned model: same tensors, same runtime, same hardware. To be clear, we haven’t joined one to a trained model. That’s the next experiment, not a result. It’s the direction we find most exciting all the same.
Decision logic you can hash
The whole policy is one file of numbers. Move it from CPU to GPU and it makes the same 1,731 decisions in the same order; feed it a recorded build and it replays it exactly. That’s how we compared v1 and v2 decision by decision in the section on making it cheaper. You can diff it, sign it, and show that a given build came from it. In fairness, ordinary code with a lockfile gets you most of the way. What the tensor version adds is that the thing running the policy is the same fixed loop of lookups and arithmetic for any program you compile into it, and a smaller runtime is a smaller thing to trust.
One more thing in its favour: the cost shrinks when the decisions are a thin layer over heavy tools. In a full ZXing build, javac and JUnit do most of the work, which is why the network costs about one and a half times the Python time there instead of twenty-odd times. Glue logic around expensive steps pays that same modest price.
Wrong tool for

Faster builds, or anything where milliseconds matter
Throwing more GPU at the problem
Replacing Maven

Worth a look for

Testing interpretability tools against a network with a known answer
Exact subroutines living next to learned models
Decision logic you can hash, replay and compare

What we’re not claiming
This isn’t all of Maven. It handles one build (clean package) of one real project, with Enforcer, Checkstyle, Javadoc and source JARs skipped. Signing, deployment and everything that only runs in verify are out of scope. The plugins aren’t neural: javac, JUnit, bnd and zip run as ordinary programs.
This isn’t machine learning. The weights were compiled from a program, not learned. We didn’t try a trained version, and we’d expect one to fail on projects it hadn’t seen.
Check our work
The weights, the runtime and the full results are on Hugging Face at shirman/neural-maven: the method, all eleven scenarios, memory use, the environment and evidence hashes, plus the raw measurements, both protocols, the analysis code and checksums. That’s enough to recompute every number in this post.

posts.title: Junie Local Comes to the NVIDIA RTX Spark
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
Junie Local is supported on the NVIDIA RTX Spark from day one, and Windows support moves from experimental to stable.

Junie Local runs alongside LLM training on the same RTX Spark laptop



NVIDIA’s RTX Spark platform pairs a Blackwell RTX GPU with a Grace CPU to run larger local AI models in slim laptops and compact desktops. Junie Local leverages this hardware to bring local AI coding to your everyday workflows.
Install Junie and run /local, and you have a full coding agent on your RTX Spark. It reads your code, edits files, and runs your tests. No token charges, no quotas, and your code never leaves the machine.
We thank NVIDIA for giving us early access to the RTX Spark and for working with us to get Junie Local ready for launch.
What the RTX Spark changes for Junie Local
In our testing on the RTX Spark, Junie Local reached generation speeds of up to 55 tokens per second. This is our initial performance baseline for the platform, with further inference optimizations already in development.
Bringing Junie Local to the RTX Spark meant adapting both setup and inference to the hardware. Junie Local automatically sizes the context window to fit the memory available to the GPU in your configuration. With more memory available, it can retain more code, tool outputs, and conversation history in its running context.
For inference, Junie Local uses Blackwell’s Tensor Cores for efficient FP8 computation, helping it process that context faster. It also uses speculative decoding to accelerate generation by drafting several tokens ahead and verifying them together.
Junie Local is now stable on Windows
When we launched Junie Local in August, it needed an M5 Mac with 64 GB of memory. We said then that lowering that bar was what we were focusing our efforts on, and that we were looking at making it runnable on 24 GB cards.
In September, we shipped experimental Windows support for NVIDIA RTX cards with 24 GB of VRAM. Today, that support is stable. If you have an Ampere or newer 24 GB RTX card, such as an RTX 3090, 4090 or 32 GB 5090 – you can run Junie Local.
Since the September preview, we’ve rebuilt the installer and the local engine. Junie Local is now ready for everyday use on:
NVIDIA RTX Spark PCs, running natively on Windows on Arm.
Windows PCs with NVIDIA RTX graphics and at least 24 GB of VRAM, running x64 Windows.
What changed:
Simple setup. The installer recognizes your PC, checks your GPU and driver, and installs an optimized inference engine, the model, and the Junie integration.
Context sized for your GPU. Junie Local picks the largest context window your GPU memory can hold.
Your choice of model. Choose Qwen3.6-27B or Qwen3.8-3.6-27B-blend, our merged model. The latter retains much of Qwen3.8’s coding ability and Qwen3.6’s shorter reasoning. Support for additional models is coming.
More reliable everyday use. The local engine starts, stops, and updates without fuss, and long coding sessions hold up better.
Requirements

PCWhat you need

NVIDIA RTX SparkWindows 11 on Arm, with at least 24 GB of memory available to the GPU
Windows PC with NVIDIA RTX graphicsWindows 11 on x64 and an NVIDIA RTX GPU with at least 24 GB of VRAM





You’ll also need NVIDIA driver 581 or newer and about 20 GB of free disk space to support the model.
Get started
In PowerShell, run:
powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -Command "[Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable('JUNIE_LOCAL_MODEL', '1', 'Process'); iex (irm 'https://junie.jetbrains.com/install.ps1')"
Then start Junie, run /model, and pick a model. Junie will download what it needs, start the local engine, and switch your session over.
What’s next
We’re working to give you more choice in local models and make them better suited to coding with Junie. That includes improving coding performance while reducing the time and memory needed to complete a task.
For the RTX Spark, we’re exploring more efficient model formats and improving speculative decoding to make better use of the GPU’s compute capacity. We’ll share benchmarks and what we learn as these improvements reach Junie Local.
Try it
Junie Local is free. No registration, no subscription, no credits, no card. Try it on supported hardware and tell us what worked, what didn’t, and what you’d like to see next.
Try Junie Local →

posts.title: Google Summer of Code 2026 With the Kotlin Foundation: Recap
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
Google Summer of Code 2026 has wrapped up! This was the Kotlin Foundation’s fourth year participating in GSoC, bringing new contributors into the Kotlin open-source ecosystem through hands-on projects and mentorship.
This year, two projects successfully reached completion, tackling two areas of the ecosystem: improving recursion support in the Kotlin/Wasm backend and building a global picture of where Kotlin is taught.
Congratulations to Ayako Hayasaka and Mark Seif Khalil, and a huge thank-you to our mentors for supporting them throughout the program!
Here’s more on what they accomplished.
Tail call support in the Kotlin/Wasm backend
Contributor: Ayako Hayasaka
Mentor: Charlie Zhang (JetBrains)
Ayako’s project added support for WebAssembly tail-call instructions to the Kotlin/Wasm backend. The compiler can now detect calls in tail position and emit return_call or return_call_ref, helping recursive Kotlin/Wasm programs avoid increasing the call stack.
In Ayako’s benchmarks, several recursive patterns became 1.7–4.3x faster at a recursion depth of 10,000. At a depth of one million, the same programs crashed without tail calls and completed successfully with them.
Testing the change on real-world projects also revealed an unexpected performance regression in V8. Ayako traced it to a missing optimization for return_call, submitted a fix, and had the patch merged into V8.
    
“What surprised me the most was that Ayako, after implementing the new WebAssembly instructions and using them in the Kotlin backend, actually found a bug in the Google V8 engine. Not only did she report the bug, she fixed it as well.”

            
Charlie Zhang
                                                        
Ayako has continued working on follow-up optimizations and other approaches to supporting recursive code beyond the original GSoC project.
For Ayako, GSoC 2026 was also a chance to work much more closely on language and runtime internals than in her everyday work.
“In my day job, I rarely get to touch the internals of a language, so I simply had a lot of fun with this opportunity. While investigating the slowdown, I had to read not only the compiler but also V8, and I realized how much there is to learn beyond the code I usually work on.”

            
Ayako Hayasaka
                                                        
Read Ayako’s full story → Final project report
Mapping the global Kotlin education landscape
Contributor: Mark Seif Khalil
Mentors: Ksenia Shneyveys (JetBrains) and Elizaveta Artser (JetBrains)
Mark’s project set out to create a structured overview of where and in what context Kotlin is being taught, considering that the information is spread across websites, course curricula, repositories, learning platforms, and other sources. The project brought that fragmented information together and created a structured and automated way to gather this data.
Over the course of GSoC 2026, Mark explored different sources and approaches to collecting this information, built a database, and developed a process for parsing and structuring data from multiple sources. 
“The biggest thing I learned is when to stop pushing on something that is not working and change my approach. This is a lesson I will keep with me in every project.”

            
Mark Seif Khalil
                                                        
The resulting project gives us a reusable foundation for monitoring Kotlin’s presence in education and identifying trends and gaps.
“What impressed us both the most about Mark was his ability to take an initially exploratory idea and bring his own vision for the research while continuously incorporating our feedback. Mark turned this scattered information into a resource we can actually use to understand Kotlin education worldwide.”

            
Ksenia Shneyveys, Elizaveta Artser
                                                        
Read Mark’s full story → Kotlin Education Landscape

Join the #gsoc channel in the Kotlin Slack to meet the community, ask questions, and follow future GSoC announcements.

posts.title: IntelliJ IDEA’s Java and Kotlin for Cursor and VS Code Hits 1.0
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
Ten weeks ago, we opened up a preview of an LSP-powered extension that brings IntelliJ IDEA’s smartness for Java and Kotlin into VS Code and Cursor. As mentioned in that blog post, this is part of a bigger initiative: moving our JVM intelligence to wherever our users are, no matter what editor or agent they are using.
Today, we’re proud to announce 1.0, the first stable release of Java and Kotlin by IntelliJ IDEA.
And we’re not shipping it alone. This release is also the result of a close collaboration with the team at Cursor, who have worked alongside us to make Java and Kotlin a first-class experience in their development environment. 






Get Java and Kotlin by IntelliJ IDEA from Visual Studio Marketplace
Get Java and Kotlin by IntelliJ IDEA from Open VSX Registry
Why this matters
Agentic development is changing how software gets built. As agents take on more implementation work, developers spend less time manually editing code – and when they do edit, they often need only a focused set of features: navigating to declarations, finding references, code completion, and renames.
These capabilities are exactly what the Language Server Protocol was built for: implementing language support once, and reusing it in any LSP-capable editor. And it’s not only humans who benefit. Agents can call into an LSP directly, producing faster, more deterministic results – and, importantly, consuming fewer tokens.
These are the workflows we want to accommodate with our extension and the underlying IntelliJ IDEA’s Language Server and Debug Adapter.
Cursor collaboration
When we set out to bring IntelliJ IDEA’s language intelligence beyond our own IDE, Cursor was a natural first partner. 
Their team collaborated closely with us throughout the development of the extension, battle-testing it and making sure Java and Kotlin developers get a seamless experience inside Cursor from the moment they open a project. 
We’re glad to work with JetBrains to bring Java and Kotlin language intelligence to Cursor. With Java and Kotlin by IntelliJ IDEA, developers get IntelliJ IDEA’s code analysis, navigation, and refactoring while they work with Cursor’s agents.
— Rohan Shah, Product, SpaceX AI
What’s in 1.0
Java and Kotlin by IntelliJ IDEA is powered by the same Java and Kotlin language technology as the IntelliJ IDEA desktop IDE. 1.0 brings a focused set of capabilities to VS Code and Cursor, including:
Java, Kotlin, and mixed-language project support
Smart code completion, navigation, and code analysis
Refactorings and editor assistance
Maven, Gradle, and Bazel build tool support
Fast, reliable performance even on large projects and monorepos
Support for test runners right now for JUnit
Powerful debugging capabilities, including emulated breakpoints and async stack traces




The full feature list is in our documentation.
For Cursor, there is dedicated support for the Agents Window. It may use its own instance of the Language Server to provide analysis capabilities based on IntelliJ IDEA’s inspections. This includes nullability support with JSpecify and for Spring Framework’s specifics.




Getting started
Install Java and Kotlin by IntelliJ IDEA from the Visual Studio Marketplace or the Open VSX registry.
Install in Cursor
Open Cursor.
Switch to IDE mode (IDE↗).
Copy the installation command .ext install JetBrains.intellij-server
Press Ctrl/Cmd+P, paste the command, and press Enter
Or get in from Open VSX Registry
Install in VS Code
Open VS Code or another compatible editor.
Copy the installation command .ext install JetBrains.intellij-server
Press Ctrl/Cmd+P, paste the command, and press Enter.
Or get it from Visual Studio Marketplace
Once installed, open your Java or Kotlin project in VS Code or Cursor. The extension analyzes your project, imports it based on any Maven, Gradle, or Bazel build files it finds, and enables Java and Kotlin language features in the editor.
Compatibility notice
Java and Kotlin by IntelliJ IDEA includes code analysis and quick-fixes that overlap with Red Hat’s and Oracle’s Java extensions. To avoid duplicated or conflicting behavior, we recommend disabling those extensions while using ours.
We have, however, made sure that our extension works well with others, like Spring Tools from the Spring Team.
Licensing
With version 1.0, the extension moves out of its free preview phase. Using it now requires an IntelliJ IDEA Ultimate subscription after a 30-day trial period during which you can try out its full feature set for free.
The same license covers IntelliJ IDEA’s Java and Kotlin capabilities everywhere you work – the IntelliJ IDEA desktop IDE, VS Code-based editors like Cursor, and other supported environments. You can review pricing here.
Note: The license is explicitly designed for human use; we’ll release an update regarding licensing models for purely agentic use soon.
Coming next: Agentic and terminal-based workflows
Java and Kotlin by IntelliJ IDEA 1.0 in the editor is just one milestone. 
In one of the next releases, agents that you orchestrate in the Agents view in Cursor or VS Code will also be able to call the LSP directly when writing code, leading to faster, better, or cheaper results.
In parallel, we’ve been running experiments applying the same LSP- and DAP-backed intelligence to fully agentic, terminal-based workflows – think Claude Code or Codex calling directly into IntelliJ IDEA’s Java and Kotlin understanding. News on this will also be announced soon.
Feedback and support
We’re still listening – Java and Kotlin by IntelliJ IDEA 1.0 is a milestone, not the finish line. Tell us what works, what doesn’t, and what you want next. Leave a comment here, open a ticket in our issue tracker, or submit a support request using this form.
Thank you to everyone who tested the preview, and to the Cursor team for launching this with us.

posts.title: How Netflix Made AI Coding Agents More Efficient with JetBrains IDE Intelligence
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
Netflix plugged JetBrains’ headless code-intelligence engine – the same one behind IntelliJ IDEA – into Claude Code and Codex, then benchmarked it against a variety of scenarios. The details and numbers are available below.




At a glance

CompanyNetflix – Application Development Platform (ADP), GenAI Platform, and Agentic SDLC teams
ChallengeCoding agents were struggling to navigate Java/Kotlin code, especially across compiled library (JAR) boundaries
TechnologyJetBrains IDE code intelligence for Java, built on the same code-indexing engine that powers IntelliJ IDEA, run headlessly with no IDE open.
Netflix’s roleBuilt the daemon and CLI needed to make the LSP callable by an agent – infrastructure that JetBrains hadn’t shipped yet
ResultTypically 20–30% more efficient (fewer tokens, less time), and up to about 65% in the best case, on real programming tasks – the size of the gain depends on the model, the agent, and the task, generally larger for stronger models and higher effort settings
Evaluated onTwo real codebases – an internal production service and Netflix’s open-source DGS Framework – across several current coding agents and models, July–August 2026





The goal: Increase agent ROI
JetBrains and Netflix set out to give coding agents accurate, IntelliJ IDEA-grade code understanding in headless environments – with no IntelliJ IDEA instance running.
“Coding agents like Claude Code are slow and unreliable at navigating Java/Kotlin code, especially across library (JAR) boundaries. We integrated a headless JetBrains IDE’s code engine to give agents IntelliJ IDE-grade code intelligence in headless environments, with no IDE running. We created a benchmark with real programming tasks, which shows that with the JetBrains IDE’s code engine, agents are consistently more efficient – using fewer tokens and less time, with the exact gain depending on the model.”
— Paul Bakker, Staff Software Engineer, Netflix
The JAR problem Netflix is trying to solve that Paul describes above: JVM projects typically ship libraries as JAR files only, never as source. Agents have to unzip the JARs (guessing which ones matter), potentially decompile class files, then grep through that incomplete view.
The solution: JetBrains IDE intelligence
JetBrains has spent years building the code intelligence engine behind IntelliJ IDEA. It is based on a deterministic index of your project source files, including all libraries. This intelligence is now exposed via an LSP and available in VS Code-compatible editors. Netflix worked with a headless build of that engine.
The LSP alone isn’t enough for a coding agent to use directly: It’s just a server speaking a protocol, with no easy way for an agent to call it and no built-in process management to reuse a running instance between calls. Netflix closed that gap themselves using the daemon and CLI described in the next section.
Architecture in detail: Keeping the index warm
Building an index for a project takes real time, just as opening a large project in IntelliJ IDEA for the first time does. A coding agent calls the LSP in many small, fine-grained steps, and a realistic task needs several such calls. If each one spun up a fresh LSP server, every single call would incur a multi-second cold-start cost – even on a project whose index had already been built a minute earlier.
A daemon process is required to avoid the overhead of cold-starting the LSP server process on repeated calls. JetBrains is working on delivering a daemon, but no daemon was available by the time of evaluation, so Netflix has built one for their own needs:
Each tool call was short-lived and stateless – it just shelled out to the CLI.
The daemon is the part that stays up: Its session manager routes each call by project root to the matching server process, which holds that project’s index in memory.
A second call against the same project skips indexing entirely and goes straight to a warm server over stdio.
Both the daemon and CLI are developed in Java and distributed as a GraalVM executable, so there is no startup or runtime overhead from the JVM.
How Netflix measured the ROI of JetBrains IDE intelligence
To understand if (and to what extent) JetBrains IDE intelligence improves the performance of a coding agent, a benchmark suite was developed. Same model, same task, same codebase – the only variable was whether the agent could invoke the JetBrains IDE intelligence. Results are reported as the performance difference between runs with JetBrains IDE intelligence versus runs without it.
Evaluation environment and approach:

DatasetsTwo real codebases: An internal service (medium-size project) using Spring Boot 4 and Gradle.
Netflix’s own open-source DGS Framework – a public, mixed Kotlin/Java GraphQL framework.
TasksTwo task types:
Small/focused tasks where the agent attempts to understand specifics in the codebase, e.g. “where is this interface used in the project”, “what implementations exist of this interface”, “what is the structure of this class”.
Full end-to-end tasks, such as implementing a new feature, refactoring a class, or removing code.
ModelsClaude Code with Opus 5 (medium/high effort)
Claude Code with Sonnet 5 (medium/high effort)
Codex with GPT-5.6 Sol (medium/high effort)
ScoringWhile the most important metrics in the experiment were token consumption and time to completion, LLM as a judge was implemented for checking correctness. It works against a reference change set for end-to-end tasks and applies deterministic scoring metric for navigation tasks.
Outlier handlingA task that crashed, hit a budget cap, or thrashed in either arm was excluded from both, so one blow-up couldn’t skew the comparison.





The benchmarks were run multiple times to validate the results and see the effects of changes from new LSP releases.
Results
Across every model, agent, and task type tested, JetBrains IDE intelligence made coding agents more efficient overall – typically 20–30% more efficient, and up to about 65% in the best case, depending on the specific model, agent, and task. The stronger models, with higher effort, saw the largest gains. These models are more expensive, so efficiency improvements matter more, but these models are also better at using indexes effectively.
~25%
Average gain
20–30%
Typical range
~65%
Best case
Configuration
          Code navigation
          End-to-end
        
Strongest model, high effort
          ~65%
          ~24%
        
Mid model, high effort
          ~29%
          ~30%
        
Mid model, medium effort
          ~24%
          ~22%
        
Lighter configuration, high effort
          ~17%*
          ~21%
        
These numbers are a snapshot, not a fixed benchmark result. Every new model release changes how agents search, reason, and use tools, so the exact percentages will keep moving – which is why this write-up reports ranges rather than per-model results. What held up across Netflix’s runs is the general shape: every model and agent tested became more efficient, the largest gains came from the strongest model at a high-effort setting, and the size of the gain differed noticeably from one model to the next.
Code-navigation tasks: More efficient across the board, correctness held or improved
Every model and effort level tested used fewer tokens with JetBrains IDE intelligence – no exceptions there – with savings ranging from roughly 15% to 60%. The size of the gain depended mostly on the model: the strongest model saw by far the largest improvements, while lighter-weight configurations landed at the lower end of both ranges. Correctness held steady in most runs and improved in two – it never dropped.
For the code-navigation tasks specifically, one tool/model combination already batches multiple search calls into a single command, so both with and without JetBrains IDE intelligence, it only makes one tool call there. Calling into JetBrains IDE intelligence is a little slower for that one call than the batched search command – which is what produced the clear lack of time benefit for that combination, not a fair reflection of real-world use. That’s why the broader end-to-end task suite is the more reliable read on time instead, where JetBrains IDE intelligence was faster across every model and agent tested.
End-to-end tasks: Consistently more efficient, correctness unaffected
On the expanded end-to-end run, correctness held steady everywhere across every model and agent tested, so the benefit shows up entirely in efficiency, not in whether the task got done. Every model and agent combination was roughly 10–30% more efficient with JetBrains IDE intelligence, looking at time to completion and token spend. A lot of this is explained by requiring fewer tool calls to come to the same conclusions.
Other evaluated alternatives
Before committing to the described approach, Netflix ruled out two others. The first rejected was a homegrown internal CLI that connected to a running IntelliJ IDEA instance to get access to a project index. The process is similar to what this article describes, but it requires an IDE to be running. This approach didn’t fit headless agents for environments like Otto, Bitbot, distributed refactoring tooling, CI, etc.
Second, an existing Eclipse LSP, which is used for Java in VS Code, was considered. But for Netflix’s build system (Gradle-based), it just didn’t work.
What’s next
Where Netflix goes from here
After the test, Netflix concluded that “the benchmarks show that there is a benefit to having a deterministic intelligence layer alongside your agent”. Of course, it doesn’t cut every coding-agent task by a fixed percentage. But for this specific problem – resolving real structure across JAR boundaries – the benefit is large, holds across models, and doesn’t cost anything in correctness.
Netflix plans to run the same benchmark methodology against Python, TypeScript/JavaScript, and Go. Coding agents for those languages have similar problems. But of course, the ways libraries are downloaded in a project vary by language, so the mechanics of the issues and possible solutions differ. JetBrains plans to continue the collaboration and support this evaluation further.
JetBrains’ take: The LSP is just one step, not the destination
JetBrains IDE intelligence for Java has been tested by Netflix and is now shipped as part of the Java & Kotlin by IntelliJ IDEA extension. JetBrains also continues experiments with the LSP+CLI approach and will report the results once ready.
The LSP’s basic primitive is a position in a text document. The specification defines a position as “between two characters, like an insert cursor in an editor”. That’s a natural primitive for a human working at a keyboard. But agents don’t really think in terms of cursor locations. They ask questions about the program, like “Why is this call inside createUser() unresolved?” and “Which tests are covering this method?”, etc. It’s about understanding relationships between parts of the code rather than looking at cursor positions. And a text position is a fragile identity – inserting one character before any given position causes that position to move.
What an agent needs isn’t a sharper cursor, but a layer that provides answers formulated in the same way as the tasks themselves – i.e. in terms of symbols, diagnostics, test relations, runtime behavior – and returns enough context to reason about the answer, not just locations in a text document.
“That’s what I mean by a code engine: not another protocol that lets an agent imitate editor interaction, but a set of precise operations over program structure and execution – one that returns enough context to actually reason about the result. LSP is useful, but it shouldn’t define the final agent-facing abstraction. Build agent tooling as if the agent were a tiny human at an editor, and you force it to speak in cursor coordinates. Agents need a code engine, not a virtual editor.”
— Aleksey Stukalov, IDE Division Lead, JetBrains
The Netflix numbers prove code intelligence is worth paying for. Deciding what shape that intelligence takes is the challenge that lies ahead.

posts.title: MPS 2026.2 Release Candidate Available
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
MPS 2026.2 is almost ready! Today we’re making a release candidate build available so you can try out the upcoming release ahead of its official launch. Download MPS 2026.2 Release Candidate now:
DOWNLOAD MPS 2026.2 Release Candidate
Along with numerous bug fixes, the RC brings several key improvements to the previous 2026.2 EAP1 build.
Linux ARM64 support
MPS is now available for Linux on ARM64 (AArch64), with a matching bundled JetBrains Java Runtime.
You can also build standalone MPS-based applications (RCPs) for Linux ARM64. The Build Script Wizard now includes a Linux ARM64 distribution in its generated build scripts alongside the existing platform distributions.
TAR imports in Build Language
Build Language now supports importing archive contents directly into distribution layouts using the new import files from tar and files from tar entries.
You can import files from plain TAR archives or archives compressed with gzip or bzip2. The source can be an archive file or another TAR layout defined in the build script.
When importing into a TAR layout, symbolic links and file permissions are preserved. This is particularly useful when packaging platform-specific plugins and native libraries, as symbolic links remain links instead of becoming duplicate copies of their targets.
Archive packaging changes
MPS 2026.2 preserves symbolic links and file permissions when packaging platform-specific plugins. Previously, symbolic links were sometimes replaced with copies of their targets, causing large native libraries to be included more than once, particularly on macOS.
macOS archive distributions now use .tar.gz instead of .zip to preserve symbolic links. The Build Script Wizard generates the same archive format for standalone macOS applications.
Projectional Agent Toolkit enhancements
Projectional Agent Toolkit has received a major boost in performance and capabilities.
Performance
Your AI agents can now cut back on token usage on common tasks like DSL modeling or implementing language definitions. In our measurements using Claude Code + Opus 5 and 5.5, the savings exceeded 50%.
This improvement is the result of a substantial rework of the MPS MCP API:
Consistent parameter naming, null and default-value handling, and error reporting.
More precise descriptions in the skills and tool documentation.
Bulk operations where they provide the greatest benefit, with compact summaries instead of huge payloads.
Small read results included directly in responses, with large dumps written to files only when needed.
One-shot model validation to check full models without round-trip overhead.
Fast concept discovery using lightweight, structure-only metadata views instead of full AST dumps.
Fail-fast checks that reject invalid search scopes and mutation inputs instead of returning incomplete results.
Helper scripts included with the skills, so agents spend less time reinventing common MPS tasks.
Clearer project targeting when several MPS or IDE projects are open.
Typesystem MCP tool
The Typesystem MCP tool enables agents to:
Understand node types and typesystem messages.
Compare types and determine the expected type for a role.
Trace type calculations and debug typesystem rules.
Identify the typesystem rule responsible for a reported typesystem error.

Other newly added MCP tools
In addition to the Typesystem MCP tool, we’ve added several more MCP tools to cover other core aspects of MPS development. The new tools enable agents to:
Invoke intentions and quick-fixes.
Automatically keep their skill database up to date with the MPS instance they connect to.
Read and filter the content of MPS logs.
Open, close, and create MPS projects.
Automatically correct SModel expressions in parsed Java statements, helping agents author concept functions and behavior methods.

Import dialog reworked: Select models and languages to import
The Import dialog has undergone a major overhaul to fix functional issues and bring its appearance in line with the rest of the platform.
When pasting code between models, only the models and languages you actually select in the dialog are imported. Previously, the dialog ignored your selection.
If the dialog offers only one suggestion, you can now deselect it. Previously, the single suggestion could not be deselected.
Both the model and language lists now have checkboxes for individual entries and a header checkbox to select or deselect all entries. The header checkbox shows an indeterminate state when only some entries are selected.
Diff dialog and tab improvements
We’ve made quite a few minor changes to bring the Diff dialog’s look and feel in line with the rest of the platform.
The model viewer now has its own icon instead of sharing the side-by-side icon. The top bar is vertically centered, and the left and right panels match the splitter background.
Diffs of added or deleted models and of per-root persistence models now have aligned title bars, so separator lines no longer drift when one side is empty.
Change markers on the scrollbar now remain in the right position when the dialog or editor is resized. Previously, a marker would sometimes jump to an unrelated location. The fix was made in the shared editor gutter, so regular editor error and warning markers are covered, too.
Editor hints defined in your language now appear on the left (read-only) diff panel for file-per-root persistence and on the right panel for per-root persistence models.
You can review the complete list of fixed issues here.
Your JetBrains MPS team
